title: Islamophobia Is Trump’s Closing Midterm Gambit
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
They say that patriotism is the last refuge of a scoundrel, but President Trump and his allies have found a new low: open bigotry against Muslims

The bar for what can shock has been raised steadily over the past decade, but even by Trump-era standards, remarks that the president made yesterday at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, are astonishing: a straightforward assertion that a Muslim candidate for office is a terrorist by virtue of his faith
Trump was campaigning for Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for U.S

Senate in Michigan, when he attacked Rogers’s opponent, the Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Trump said. “If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.” Trump also said that “anyone with that record of support for jihadists would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane.” He added that if elected, El-Sayed “would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.” (In fact, the only time that members of Congress have had to pass through metal detectors in the Capitol was on the House side, as a security precaution after Trump supporters sacked it on January 6, 2021.) To be clear: El-Sayed has disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, and no one has produced any evidence that he has ties to the group
Neither has anyone produced any evidence that El-Sayed has ties to any jihadists or is one himself
If he did, the Justice Department would presumably be prosecuting him—it certainly hasn’t shied away from politicized cases under Trump
The president and anyone else are free to critique El-Sayed’s views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, or any other policy matter, but that’s not what this is

Asking a candidate to disavow a foreign political group that has no American arm is a nonsensical and prejudiced thing to do, but Republicans have been trying hard in the past couple of weeks to draw some connection between El-Sayed and the group, despite a lack of evidence. (They have been assisted by allies in the press, including Bari Weiss, the editor in chief of CBS News, whose staffers complained to Semafor that she is disproportionately focused on candidates such as El-Sayed because of her own views on Israel
CBS News called the report “baseless.”) Perhaps this is because they believe “Muslim Brotherhood” sounds shadowy and scary to voters
The new tack is also silly because the GOP previously spent months trying to connect El-Sayed to the Democratic Socialists of America, another group that he says he is not a member of
Historically, the Brotherhood, an Islamist organization, has typically clashed with socialists in the Muslim world
Trump’s idea of what a senator should be is an older white man
That’s not a guess—it’s what he said about Rogers, the Republican candidate. “I call him apple pie,” Trump said. “He’s like, perfect, this guy
He’s what your state is all about.” As I’ve written in the past, it’s not a dog whistle if everyone can hear it
Trump has also made light of El-Sayed’s full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, mocking the prevalence of Muhammad in Muslim names. (The president’s own middle name is John.) “Donald Trump and J

Vance, their whole campaign, Mike Rogers’s whole campaign, is to point at me and my name and my faith,” El-Sayed said in response at a rally yesterday evening. “But my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas
My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your groceries
My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t see a doctor.” Trump’s latest remarks about El-Sayed are of a piece with a series of racist and Islamophobic remarks
Two frequent targets of late are Representative Ilhan Omar, the Minnesota Democrat, and the Somali community in Minnesota
He has called Omar “garbage” and said that Somalia is “filthy, dirty, disgusting, dirty.” He has labeled Somalis “low-IQ” but also complained that they are highly effective grifters
Politicians allied with Trump are also getting in on the hate
Earlier this year, I wrote about a spree of bigoted remarks by GOP members of Congress

More recently, Representative Tom Emmer, a Minnesota Republican, said that Somali Americans should assimilate or “go the hell back.” (He added that he wasn’t afraid of being called an Islamophobe.) And Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who is in a tough reelection race, falsely claimed that his Democratic opponent, Gina Hinojosa, “supports Sharia law” because she received an endorsement from the Council on American-Islamic Relations
You don’t have to think too hard to guess why CAIR opted to back someone running against Abbott

With this kind of talk, it’s no wonder that Muslim voters who backed Trump in 2024, largely out of frustration with the Biden administration’s policies toward Israel, are now angry and disillusioned, as The New York Times reports . (Anyone is entitled to cast a protest vote, but given Trump’s long record of anti-Muslim bigotry, those who lined up behind Trump shouldn’t be surprised.) Islamophobic rhetoric deserves condemnation on its own terms, but the attacks don’t just affect El-Sayed, Omar, or even Muslim communities in the United States

During the same speech, Trump—who has previously said that Jewish Democrats are “disloyal to Jewish people” —called for ostracizing any Jewish Michiganders who vote for El-Sayed. “Any Jewish person that supports this guy should be ashamed of themselves,” he said . “You should never speak to them again.” Once bigotry against one community enters the mainstream, it tends to spread quickly to other groups

title: Yes, We Have No Bananas
excerpt: Maybe you’ve seen the ad: A man and a woman are loading a shopping cart
body: Maybe you’ve seen the ad: A man and a woman are loading a shopping cart

The woman tells the man he must return a carton of eggs. “We have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians.” The woman explains that grocery prices are rising because the United States gives so much aid to Israel. “It’s costing us a lot of money to drop bombs on Gaza,” the woman explains. “Don’t they get universal health care too?” the man asks. “We’re paying for that, too, probably,” the woman responds, at which point the man puts back the bananas
The ad was produced by an independent political-action committee to support the Senate campaign of the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed
During the Democratic primary, El-Sayed regularly denounced American supporters of Israel as a shadowy, sinister special interest
Since winning the nomination, he has distanced himself from his earlier language
Now a super PAC is reviving it for him only a week before the general election
Thompson explained the ad half a century before it was produced

In his book Fear and Loathing on the Campaign Trail ’72 , he described “one of the oldest and most effective tricks in politics,” which may have played a role in one of Lyndon Johnson’s early campaigns in Texas: The race was close and Johnson was getting worried

Finally he told his campaign manager to start a massive rumor campaign about his opponent’s life-long habit of enjoying carnal knowledge of his own barnyard sows. “Christ, we can’t get away calling him a pig-fucker,” the campaign manager protested. “Nobody’s going to believe a thing like that.” “I know,” Johnson replied. “But let’s make the sonofabitch deny it.” In the case of the ad supporting El-Sayed, the sonofabitch targeted by the false accusation is not El-Sayed’s theoretical opponent, the Republican Mike Rogers—not really

The ad concludes, “Mike Rogers is for”—ironic chuckle—“they/them.” We all know who they are, and they are the real target of the ad. [ James Loeffler: The hatred that broke American politics ] The accusation that Israel is to blame for America’s economic problems is not some unique quirk of El-Sayed supporters

During his campaign to become New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani told Politico in 2025 that the dilapidated state of the city’s housing was the fault of the same villain: “The government refuses to fund public housing, all while we continue to find billions of dollars to drop bombs that kill tens of thousands of Palestinians over more than a year now.” That same year, Marjorie Taylor Greene drew a similar link

American aid, she charged , typically accounts for up to a fifth of Israel’s defense budget, “even though Israel, nuclear-armed Israel, has universal healthcare for their citizens and subsidized college for their citizens

Here in America, we’re $37 trillion in debt.” On Meet the Press in August, El-Sayed insinuated that U.S. aid for weapons in Israel was somehow an impediment to health care at home. “This campaign was a referendum on whether or not we want health care here or bombs somewhere else.” Do supporters of Israel have to deny the false accusation? Okay, here goes
U.S. military aid to Israel is set at $3.8 billion a year from 2019 to 2028—about one-20th of 1 percent of the total federal budget

In 2024, Congress approved a $95 billion aid package for Ukraine, Israel, and other allies—of which, nearly two-thirds went to Ukraine, about $15 billion went to Israel, and about $9 billion was directed to humanitarian relief, including assistance for Gazan civilians displaced by the war that Hamas started. (The rest went to Taiwan and other allies in the Indo-Pacific region.) Almost all U.S. assistance to Israel takes the form of credits that Israel can use only to buy American-made equipment
This assistance provides at least two direct and immediate benefits to Americans
First, it buys the United States access to Israeli military technology
By partly underwriting the development of Israel’s Iron Dome missile-defense system, the U.S. has gained the use of battle-tested systems that also protect American lives
Second, this assistance lowers the per-unit cost of U.S. systems
The United States buys up to 48 F-35 fighters a year
Israel has bought 75 and is considering an estimated 25 more
Foreign orders allow U.S. arms manufacturers to improve their economies of scale

At a time when other NATO allies are canceling their orders of American equipment because they no longer fully trust the U.S. as an ally or supplier, Israeli orders enhance the efficiency of American defense production. [ Helen Lewis: The firebrand ] Meanwhile, all U.S. aid to Israel amounts to a fraction of what Israel’s critics wish to spend domestically
Despite the implications of that El-Sayed ad: Americans spend $1.1 trillion a year on groceries
Canceling aid to Israel would deliver the equivalent of about 30 hours of that spending

Per Mamdani’s complaint that Israel is to blame for bad housing in New York City: The city’s housing authority estimates its backlog of deferred maintenance at almost $80 billion, or about 20 years’ worth of U.S. assistance to Israel at present levels
Expanding Medicare to cover all American citizens would cost perhaps more than $32 trillion in additional federal spending over the first decade
Covering even one month of this plan would take 70 years’ worth of aid to Israel
By blaming the Jewish state for the price of bananas in Michigan, the super-PAC ad calls to mind political tricks older and more disturbing than the one attributed to Johnson

In 1899, Karl Lueger, the mayor of Vienna and one of the most notorious anti-Semites of the 19th century, gave a speech blaming the Habsburg empire’s economic troubles on its Jews. “Here in our Austrian fatherland the situation is such that the Jews have seized a degree of influence which exceeds their number and importance,” he argued. “And in this respect the Jews operate a terrorism of a kind that could hardly be worse
For us, in Austria, it is a matter of liberating Christian people from the hegemony of Jewry.” As with the rising cost of living in the U.S., the problem Lueger was concerned with was real
His voter base of artisans and craftspeople was coming under immense pressure from factory competition
There was not much Lueger could do about his voters’ distress
But he could point them toward a politically useful target
Now, with a modest update of Lueger’s language, an outside PAC’s closing argument in one of the most watched Senate races of 2026 blames a familiar “they/them.”

title: How Long Until the Internet Breaks?
excerpt: On Wednesday, July 18, 2001, a freight train derailed in Baltimore’s Howard Street Tunnel
body: On Wednesday, July 18, 2001, a freight train derailed in Baltimore’s Howard Street Tunnel

Flammable liquid ignited, causing a fire that raised the temperature in the tunnel to 1,000 to 1,500 degrees. “We’re told some of the boxcars are actually glowing,” a fire-department spokesperson told the Associated Press
More than 100 firefighters were called to fight the blaze
The National Transportation Safety Board investigated the fire but never figured out what went wrong
No one was killed, and other trains were rerouted to avoid the inferno
But more than trains navigated the tunnel’s brick-­lined walls: Several internet-service providers and telecommunications companies were running cables through it
The internet couldn’t be so easily retransmitted
The cables that wound their way through the tunnel were damaged, and web traffic as far away as Atlanta and Los Angeles slowed to a crawl
One company that measures web performance said“the internet delays were the worst it had seen,” reported the Associated Press
A single tunnel was responsible for much of the country’s web traffic, and Americans paid the price
It is physical, subject to the vagaries of nature and time, just as our bodies are
The internet’s fragility crops up everywhere: in the sudden disappearance of a relied-­upon website, and in the endless thrum of posts, images, and videos
In the case of the Howard Street Tunnel, the fragility became, without warning, quite obvious

As the writer Maria Farrell and the technologist Robin Berjon note in their 2024 essay titled “ We Need to Rewild the Internet ,” WorldCom—a ­major phone-and-internet company at the time—played an important role in the outages that followed the inferno. “WorldCom had spread web traffic over different fiber networks,” they write, but “the region’s narrow physical topography had concentrated all those different fiber networks into a single chokepoint, the Howard Street Tunnel
WorldCom’s resilience was, quite literally, incinerated

It had technological redundancy, but not diversity.” Despite dealing in the physical world—in the fiber-­optic cables that make up the real, material internet—WorldCom had somehow forgotten that the land makes its own rules
Efficiencies can be found in transmitting data through companies that consolidate the services we need to be online
In 2021, Fastly, a cloud-utility provider, stopped working for an hour, taking down the websites of major news outlets including CNN, The New York Times , and The Guardian
The Verge , a technology-news site, ended up publishing updates about the outage via Google Docs while its website was down

The day of the disruption, Fastly’s stock price actually rose. “Investors were delighted by headlines that informed them of an obscure technical service provider with an apparent lock on an essential service,” Farrell and Berjon write. “To investors, this critical infrastructure failure doesn’t look like fragility but like a chance to profit.” Fragility and profit go hand in hand, which makes some sense when you remember that corporate redundancy always carries inefficiency
Brittleness is big business, a feature and not a bug of the cloud economy
But the cloud obscures the very real collection of companies, people, and processes that create and structure the internet

When we put something in the cloud, we don’t just offload the responsibility of maintaining our data to fickle chunks of magnetic metal alight with electricity; we also offload that responsibility to a rather limited set of fickle human institutions

You might want your family photos to live in the cloud for centuries, but “most companies do not last long,” Maxwell Neely-­Cohen wrote for the Harvard Law School’s Library Innovation Lab. “They get acquired or split up into pieces or go bankrupt or decline into something much smaller or are upended by catastrophic geopolitical events.” [ Read: Inside the dirty, dystopian world of AI data centers ] The cloud also shrouds the cables, data centers, and transmission towers that compose the internet itself. “The cloud is made possible by a relatively small number of undersea cables that require constant maintenance,” continued Neely-­Cohen
For a medium so often praised as decentralized, for a metaphor that calls to mind something diffuse, that’s an awful lot of centralization

A small number of companies own the data centers, connected by a small number of cables also owned by a small number of companies, through which data, yet again owned by a small number of companies, flow
The internet, in this telling, looks much more like the Howard Street Tunnel than a cloud
And now artificial intelligence has gusted in, revealing the physical infrastructure that the cloud used to hide

Ordinary people can see more clearly than ever the precarity of the supply chains and the power of the chips that fill the water-guzzling, electricity-hungry data centers that so many have come to loathe
Just as AI reveals the physicality of our digital lives, it has also brought into sharp focus the crucial pieces of software that undergird the internet
Last week, an AI model found security vulnerabilities in PHP , a coding language used in 70 percent of websites
Despite its centrality to the modern web, I’d hazard a guess that PHP isn’t a household name
Originally named as an acronym for personal homepage , it was built to help host its creator’s résumé

As PHP grew in popularity, it shed some of that DIY spirit—and that acronym—but, like so many essential systems that keep the web online, volunteers remain an essential part of its maintenance . [ Read: ‘If anything happens to this guy … everyone is screwed’ ] In a classic comic about the state of modern infrastructure, a precarious Jenga tower is held up by a single block labeled “a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003.” AI—swarming onto rarely used Wikipedia pages, probing poorly run government websites, discovering zero-day exploits—has shown the web to be the frail, uncanny place that it has always been
Indeed, the most cloudlike part of this state of affairs is the absence of human agency
As users of the web, we have to pay attention to the data and infrastructure that the cloud cloaks
Hordes of flesh-­and-­blood engineers, sitting in glass-­and-­steel office buildings and water-­and-­air-­cooled data centers, attend to the systems that hold our words, pictures, and videos
What we store and what we transmit are acts of attention to a world that remains resolutely material, despite the seeming immateriality of our digital lives
Human institutions remain central to the practice of storage and transmission—an inconvenient fact, because human institutions fade, just as human bodies do
The cloud is refreshed every moment of every day by the fresh attention of humans

title: Red States Are Dumbing Down College Admissions
excerpt: ET on October 26, 2026 N othing makes me more nauseated than a row of multiple-choice questions and empty bubbles
body: ET on October 26, 2026 N othing makes me more nauseated than a row of multiple-choice questions and empty bubbles
After I turned 18, I thought I’d never encounter that feeling again, outside of stress dreams about forgetting my No. 2 pencils

And yet there I was, hiding in a cubicle at work to take a test intended for high schoolers, demonstrating my understanding of apostrophe placement and verb tense, and comparing the definition of truth in passages from Nietzsche and JFK
I was taking the Classic Learning Test, an alternative to the SAT and ACT
The test is only 11 years old, and was originally taken mainly by kids who were homeschooled or had attended private religious academies

But use of the test is growing at an astonishing pace in red states where there’s a belief that the SAT and ACT have neglected the Western canon in an attempt to become “woke.” In the past three years, public universities in Florida, Arkansas, Texas, Georgia, Indiana, and Iowa announced that applicants could submit their CLT scores in place of SAT and ACT results
Oklahoma, Louisiana, and Wyoming now allow students to use their CLT scores to qualify for state scholarships
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recently called it the “gold standard” exam, and starting this year, military-service academies will accept CLT scores too
Some 200,000 kids will take the test this year

As a remedial-English teacher at a public high school in New York, and then a college-admissions counselor in Maryland, he had become disillusioned with the American education system and what he saw as its emphasis on preparing students for the workforce. “What every other generation was doing in education was fundamentally a different kind of project,” he told me
They were doing two things: “moral formation” and the “transmission of this cultural, intellectual, Western inheritance.” College-entrance exams inform high-school curricula
Because the SAT and ACT emphasize rote reading and math skills, that’s much of what schools teach
But if students had to take a classical-learning test, Tate believed, schools would be forced to teach the Western canon
In 2015, Tate opened the for-profit Classic Learning Initiatives and started administering the CLT
Students are recorded as they take the two-hour test online, to prevent cheating
The exam is divided into three sections: verbal reasoning, grammar and writing, and math
Most of the texts are taken from a list of classics beginning with The Epic of Gilgamesh and ending with Toni Morrison
The math section covers algebra, geometry, trigonometry, and mathematical reasoning
Tate presents the CLT as more rigorous than the SAT and the ACT
The CLT is the only one that doesn’t allow calculators, and its reading passages are longer than those on the SAT
But his biggest sell is on the substance of the texts

The other tests, he argues, have altered their content to push “anti-Western left-wing ideology.” (Representatives for the ACT and SAT denied that the tests had any ideological leaning, or any agenda beyond assessing college readiness

Granted, it’s been several years since I took either one, but I recall more questions about the definition of words such as zenith and benediction than any progressive polemics.) [ Idrees Kahloon: Actually, the SAT was necessary ] Tate’s objection is a bit surprising when you remember that, for years, criticism of the SAT and ACT has mainly been a left-wing phenomenon

Some progressives oppose all standardized testing as inequitable, giving an unfair advantage to children from wealthy backgrounds and cutting students with lower scores off from future opportunities, while also failing to measure qualities such as creativity and grit
During the beginning of the pandemic, in 2020, many universities, including all of the Ivy League schools, made the SAT and ACT optional for applications
But since then, most top schools have reinstated the test requirements, finding that they’re the most reliable way to predict students’ abilities
Now, suddenly, the tests are being attacked from the other side
Eventually, Tate intends for his test to dwarf the SAT and ACT
He has a long way to go; last year, 2 million graduating seniors had taken the SAT at some point during high school, and 1.4 million had taken the ACT
More than two dozen states, about half of which have Republican leaders, have all public-school students take the SAT or ACT

But Tate believes that Americans are waking up to the testing companies’ “hollowing out and politicization” of schools. “I think word is getting out more and more among students that the SAT and ACT just aren’t really serious,” he told me

Although Harvard and MIT do not accept the CLT, Tate said that a growing number of students are submitting CLT scores to impress their admissions offices. (An MIT spokesperson told me over email that CLT scores are not considered in admissions decisions
The not was underlined.) Tate claims that the CLT, in contrast to the SAT and ACT, is not political
Yes, Christopher Rufo, the anti-critical-race-theory activist, is on the board of Classic Learning Initiatives

But so is Cornel West, the public intellectual who calls himself a “non-Marxist socialist.” “He’s a good friend,” Tate told me. (West did not reply to a request for comment.) There’s nothing partisan, Tate argues, about valuing rigor and revering old books

Recently, the CLT’s X account posted a collage celebrating what it called “arguably the 50 most influential books in history.” The image appears to be AI-generated; it includes The Aeneid by “Virmer.” F or the first eight years of its existence, only about 20,000 students took the CLT
But in 2023, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis got into a fight with the College Board over its AP African American Studies course, which he accused of indoctrinating students in left-wing ideology
Florida began to allow high-school students to use their CLT score to apply to the state’s public universities and its biggest scholarship program
Among students who weren’t destined for college, those who failed Florida’s end-of-semester exams could use a CLT score to fulfill their English and math graduation requirements
Over the next two years, Florida’s high-school graduation rate increased by four percentage points

title: Leave the Cheesecake Factory Out of This
excerpt: A t 2 o’clock on Sunday afternoon, I found myself in a corner booth at the Cheesecake Factory, emerging from the fog of war
body: A t 2 o’clock on Sunday afternoon, I found myself in a corner booth at the Cheesecake Factory, emerging from the fog of war
Before me were a dozen half-empty plates, a cluster of dirty napkins, and several depleted beverages
The food had come in waves, unrelenting, like Normandy

There had been egg rolls, four ways; Roadside Sliders; a sheet tray of Factory Nachos; and something called Chicken Parmesan “Pizza Style.” Coke Zeros , I’d told the waitress at the beginning, and keep ’em coming
But another feeling, too, was detectable within the churning volcano of my digestive tract: It was something like joy
Over the weekend, Barack Obama criticized President Trump’s schlocky White House aesthetic by saying it looked like “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” My first reaction was to laugh
It’s true! The restaurant is over-the-top opulent—as if ancient Egypt and Tuscany had a baby in Las Vegas
Any true Cheesecake Factory fan would certainly appreciate the joke, especially if they remembered the Iraq War and Saddam’s own design sensibilities
What happened next, though, was disheartening. “Hasn’t eaten dinner that costs less than $250 in years

Has never been in a Cheesecake Factory,” the conservative commentator Scott Jennings wrote on X. “Undefeated at condescending to regular folks.” Other Republicans, and even some Democrats, logged on to police the former president’s tone
This was classic elitist Obama, they argued, making fun of the working man and his primitive taste
It was why Trump won and why Democrats will never win back blue-collar America
My “For You” page filled with commentary about which political party could more confidently claim ideological custody over the Cheesecake Factory
Immediately, my head began to swirl like the raspberry drizzle in a Georgia Peach cocktail
My rage was congealing, like Cheddar Cheese Fondue on room-temperature Pretzel Bites

Leave the Cheesecake Factory out of your culture wars ! Like any number of kitschy, charming American chain restaurants—Rainforest Cafe, Johnny Rockets, and even, God love it, Applebee’s—the Factory can obviously be mocked
But it must be mocked from a place of love
It should exist above partisan politics as a sacred third space, one of the few we Americans have left
Quickly enough, my frustration gave way to hunger, then introspection, and then to investigatory zeal

Which is how, an hour later, I ended up at the Cheesecake Factory. (I was helped along the path by my editor, who said I could expense everything.) M y friends joined me at the restaurant, a block from the White House
No one asked why we were rushing to get a table
It wasn’t busy—just a handful of tourists and families—and we were seated quickly in a quiet corner, where James Blunt emerged softly from the speaker system

I looked around at the design, which I had seen plenty of times but never quite absorbed before: There were orange faux-marble ceiling beams, trellis-patterned dividers, and columns with faux-tile inlay
The vibe was vaguely Italian, loosely Moorish
There were no gilded trophies or signs , but I could see Obama’s point
I explained his joke to our waitress, who seemed about 20 and well adjusted enough to not be spending time on X
She laughed. “Oh, damn, we caught a stray!” she said. “That’s funny, though
Maybe that’s why we’re slow this morning.” I knew that I loved the Cheesecake Factory before I ever went inside one. “Too expensive,” my mother would say before steering me toward the food court

But peering through the windows of the restaurant at Jordan Creek Town Center in Des Moines, I was awed by its sumptuousness: the orange, inviting glow from the knobbly chandeliers; the floral frescoes and painted columns; the generous fountain pops and the dense wedges of cake
It wasn’t attempting highbrow elegance but, rather, embracing a kind of madcap largesse, like a zany aunt who wears a lot of bracelets

Inside the Cheesecake Factory, everyone always seemed to be laughing. [ From the May 2026 issue: The best free bread in America ] Trump, Saddam, and the Cheesecake Factory share an unabashed commitment to aesthetic maximalism
To be sure, this commitment is slightly more appealing in a restaurant than in the office of a democratically elected leader of a country founded on the explicit rejection of monarchy
And there is obviously nothing appealing about Saddam’s palaces, or Saddam himself—which is why it is unfair to associate Saddam with the Cheesecake Factory in any way
I didn’t cover the Iraq War personally, being too young, but I can still promise you with a high degree of confidence that there were no Thai Lettuce Wraps on offer at the Babylon Palace
Laughter and togetherness were not, I gather, the order of the day at Qasr al-Nihayah
Still, by all accounts, Saddam appreciated food—and especially, in spite of everything, American food
He was reportedly a great lover of hamburgers

After he was tried and convicted, but before he was hanged, his guards said he could polish off entire family-size bags of Doritos. (Nacho Cheese, I’d guess.) For breakfast, he apparently delighted in Raisin Bran Crunch
Saddam might have been a happier, more reasonable dictator if he’d had a Cheesecake Factory nearby (this is what is known in journalism as a comically irrefutable assertion)
The thing about the Cheesecake Factory is that the food is not simply good

title: Netanyahu Goes Into Full Panic Mode
excerpt: When the going gets tough, the tough don’t get subtle
body: When the going gets tough, the tough don’t get subtle

Yesterday, with polls casting doubt on his continuing as Israel’s prime minister after Tuesday’s election, Benjamin Netanyahu posted a closing argument on Instagram: an AI-generated image of Tel Aviv destroyed by a nuclear blast, with accompanying text that asked, roughly, Would you prefer to reelect Netanyahu, or be incinerated along with your family? The text—written by the commentator Yuval Bloomberg and reproduced approvingly by Netanyahu—called all of the other campaign issues a “smokescreen,” and accused Netanyahu’s opponents of being so blinded by hatred that they would rather increase their chances of being burned alive than see their country’s political maestro win another election
If you support another candidate, the Instagram post cautioned, “your hand should tremble” as you vote
For years, Israelis both pro- and anti-Netanyahu have advised against counting him out
He has a Nixon-like ability to reemerge improbably stronger every time his political career has been declared over
It seemed over on October 7, 2023, when his government presided over an actual mass burning of Israelis
This time, the group of politicians cooperating to drive him from office is diverse and formidable
A former observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet, retired General Gadi Eisenkot, is his chief antagonist

But two allied former prime ministers, the centrist Yair Lapid and Naftali Bennett on the center-right, are enthusiastic members of the anti-Netanyahu coalition, and another ex-general, Yair Golan, is attacking him from what remains of the Israeli left
These combined efforts have reduced Netanyahu’s chances of remaining in power to one in four, as of this morning
These relatively long odds account, perhaps, for the wild messaging from Netanyahu during the past three days
Netanyahu’s statements have been, as George W

Bush said after Donald Trump’s “American carnage” speech, “some weird shit.” In addition to warning that his opponents will be too beholden to Islamists to stop the flattening of Tel Aviv, Netanyahu’s pronouncements include the following assertions: that it is “only a matter of time” before American military assistance for Israel is “over,” that Israel will be beset by international sanctions and compelled to cope without the friends who have in the past guaranteed its survival, and that blockchain-based technologies, such as cryptocurrencies, might provide ways around sanctions. [ Read: Defeating Netanyahu means solving a math problem ] The other candidates have positioned themselves as normal people who can govern Israel competently in difficult times

Bennett replied to the atom-bomb post by calling for the “revival of our international standing,” and declaring his intention to improve the tech sector and force thousands of Israel’s 1.5 million ultra-Orthodox citizens to trade full-time religious study for military service and employment. (Netanyahu and his further-right coalition partners have refused these measures and tried to preserve draft exemptions.) Netanyahu, Yair Lapid wrote , “has gone off the rails
We must send him home.” Netanyahu’s case is that he is an unusual man for unusual times

If the times are not unusual already, he will make them unusual, by shifting Israel’s politics and alliances preemptively—away from America and toward the United Arab Emirates, away from Western financial systems and toward crypto, in a manner reminiscent of sanctions-hobbled regimes like Russia, Iran, and North Korea
There is a logic to this frightening perspective

If you think Israel can be a liberal democracy in a familiar international order, and that competent institutions and international alliances are the way to stave off catastrophe, then vote from the menu of Netanyahu’s opponents
If you think Israel is doomed to being a pariah state, then vote for the guy posting images of his country torched in a nuclear holocaust

Today Avigdor Lieberman, the leader of the secular-nationalist Yisrael Beiteinu party and a member of the anti-Netanyahu club, requested a treason investigation into Netanyahu for intentionally “dragging Israel into war” to improve his electoral chances
This threat of annihilation is not, of course, wholly concocted
But Iran’s open desire to annihilate Israel can be real and still be used as a political pretext to avoid the issues that have led so many Israelis to hate Netanyahu

The same Instagram post that warns of nuclear annihilation helpfully lists these issues: alleged links between Netanyahu and the government of Qatar, reports that Netanyahu received warnings before the October 7 attacks and did nothing, and his support for welfare and draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox full-time Torah students
About 100,000 such ultra-Orthodox are liable for military service, and most instead study Talmud and are therefore too busy to cram themselves into tanks and fight in Gaza like other Jewish Israelis
Netanyahu’s response to all of these accusations is to crank up the end-of-days volume, to make even the most reasonable criticisms of his politics inaudible
Among secular Israelis, the last of these gripes produces such bitterness that some seem willing to die rather than vote for a politician who would preserve the exemptions

The bitterness stems from the perception that Netanyahu (himself a religious novice) is eager to make unconscionable concessions to the most extreme elements of the ultra-Orthodox political machine in exchange for a few more seats in his coalition

The main ultra-Orthodox parties are Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), both pro-Netanyahu and monomaniacal about preserving exemptions for as many Torah students as possible. [ Graeme Wood: Israel can’t postpone its reckoning forever ] The cynicism of this move is easiest to appreciate not by assaying the venom of secular Israelis but by hearing the dismay of ultra-Orthodox Israelis, also known as Haredim (those who “tremble” before God) unaligned with Shas and UTJ

Ziva Glanz, a candidate for the upstart Haredi Public party, told me with exasperation that the “legacy” parties were immune to change, and that most Haredim were ready to move on, if only the ossified political system would let them
Her party is broadly in the Netanyahu camp, and her party is happy to support Netanyahu’s view of Israel’s security. “Existential problems are existential problems,” she said
But they nonetheless want reform, and see his government and its partners as stopping it
Her party supports reducing the number of draft-exempt Torah students
Glanz, the wife of a rabbi, says she thinks the low civilian-casualty rate in Israel’s war with Hezbollah was a miracle granted by God because of Israel’s commitment to religious study

But she says there are 12,000 Haredim who purport to be studying, and whose institutions claim government funds, when in reality they are “hanging out in pizza shops.” They should be put to work. “Our community is a success,” she said, and “with success comes responsibility.” Netanyahu’s response to this modest attempt to disrupt Haredi politics and integrate Haredim into the Israeli national project has been to tell her party to back down

When Netanyahu first won the premiership in 1996, he successfully campaigned on “making a safe peace”—peace guaranteed through Israeli military supremacy, rather than primarily through the negotiation or diplomacy preferred by his rivals
Three decades later, a “safe peace” guaranteed through military might has become so strategically desirable that it unites his rivals—security hawks, one and all—while Netanyahu himself has moved on
Now he promises that his opponents will bring annihilation
In this account, Israel’s violent devastation is so imminent that corruption, pandering, and venality become mere foibles

But what if ignoring these political vices devastates Israel in slower, less lurid ways? What if limitless draft exemptions, unwillingness to scrutinize past failures, and international isolation are themselves devastating? Tomorrow Israelis will vote, many trembling for the future of their country, no matter which candidate they prefer.

title: Will the real Anthropic please stand up
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here
After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus
The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world
But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years
In fact, its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture

Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here

Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers
Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation

And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience
The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes
It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?) Take another example

Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection

We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.” Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience
When so little seems certain, what Anthropic (and its fellow frontier AI companies) say is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship

I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this. (That’s for another day.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum.  It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic? It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think

The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation

Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked ).   Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said
But why should we trust it? “What is Anthropic?” he asked

Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth.  But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that
As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free

Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because of their egos
In fact, Anthropic is all of these things

As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post : “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry
The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly
And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.” Amodei makes it sound as if he’s got it all tied up, but playing multiple roles is hard

There are huge tensions between the priorities of an AI safety organization and a profit-driven megacorp, for example. (Amodei admits in his post that he has made mistakes.) Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us
They should help us figure out how much to trust it to self-regulate or whether we should be forcing it to give external safety testers access to its models on our terms rather than theirs
They should help us give it the benefit of the doubt (or not) when what looks like a self-serving piece of legislation comes to light
But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra
Anthropic is many things to many people, and I’m not sure that makes it more trustworthy
In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read.

title: The Download: everyday AI harms and the race to nuclear spaceflight
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

Opinion: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms —Sam Hiner, cofounder of the Young People’s Alliance, and Emma Leiken, executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab We have historically allowed debates over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day
A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people
Students are relying on chatbots to write their papers, while social media feeds engineered to provoke envy keep users watching
These products can meet narrow safety requirements yet still erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another
As we enter an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than address only catastrophic harms

Are we there yet? Nuclear-powered spaceships Earlier this year, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, and fly it to Mars by the end of 2028
A successful mission could herald more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight, saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation
But nuclear space propulsion has moved slowly
The US has started—and terminated—several programs exploring the technology over the past 75 years

title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
excerpt: Consider what passes for success in technology policy
body: Consider what passes for success in technology policy
An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide
A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl
These are important protections, and they should have existed all along
But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling
We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day
As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms

We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.  A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases

Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching
A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines
A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions
Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation
Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line
It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms
Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address
This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states

The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services
Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed
This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable
We have been through a version of this with social media

Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there

No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale
Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar , anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka , and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war
The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world
AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance
It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to
A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people

MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete
There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects
We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place

Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own)
But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain

We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own.  We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more
Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms

Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves
The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline

Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119
Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list

Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs
She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

title: What legal experts say about the Trump administration’s attempts to make a federal case out of state elections

Dan Sullivan, left, narrowly loses his reelection bid, it&#39;ll be because voters mistakenly voted for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/AlaskaSenateLawsuitExplainer/a07e652f18a2413ca85d1595604cbc77/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=Alaska%20Sullivan%20&amp;currentItemNo=0&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Mark Thiessen; Becky Bohrer</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/75009254/1/united-states-v-state-of-alaska/">Trump administration’s lawsuit against Alaska</a>, which seeks to block certification of the U.S. Senate results there if the GOP candidate does not win, is the latest in a long series of actions throughout 2026 in which <a href="https://www.reuters.com/investigations/how-trump-is-moving-control-us-elections-one-state-time-2026-04-27/">the administration has attempted to wrest control of federal elections</a> from states.  </p>

<p>In the Alaska case, the U.S. Department of Justice, <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6168997-donald-trump-justice-alaska-senate-lawsuit/">directed by President Donald Trump</a>, claims that it aims to “<a href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.akd.80263/gov.uscourts.akd.80263.1.0.pdf">protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska</a>.” If incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan does not win reelection, the DOJ asserts, it’s likely the result of voter confusion because another candidate with a very similar name – <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/whats-going-on-with-dan-sullivan-and-dan-sullivan-the-alaska-senate-litigation-explained">Daniel J. Sullivan, with no party affiliation</a> – is on the ballot, too. So in the event that Sen. Sullivan fails to win reelection, the DOJ demands that Alaska not certify the election and instead should conduct an inquest into who voters thought they were voting for.</p>

<p>The campaign of the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/alaska-us-senate-election-polls-2026.html">whose potential win in the hotly contested election</a> could help shift the Senate to Democratic control, has called the lawsuit “<a href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/75009254/8/1/united-states-v-state-of-alaska/">wholly baseless</a>” and “<a href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.akd.80263/gov.uscourts.akd.80263.5.0.pdf">an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections</a>” in a court filing. Another <a href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/75009254/6/1/united-states-v-state-of-alaska/">filing states that the DOJ lawsuit</a> “asks the Court to preemptively nullify Alaska’s U.S. Senate election and disenfranchise Alaska voters without any legal basis whatsoever. It seeks to go where law ends.” </p>

<p>There’s lots of other heated language in <a href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/75009254/united-states-v-state-of-alaska/">the case’s legal filings</a>. But colorful language and legal citations are a much longer way of articulating a simple fact: The U.S. Constitution gives the president no authority over federal elections. <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/article-1/section-4/clause-1/">That authority rests with the states</a> and, <a href="https://statecourtreport.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/states-not-president-run-elections-america">to a limited degree, with Congress</a>.</p>

<p>Over the past year, as the 2026 midterm elections approached, The Conversation has published a number of stories illustrating this fundamental constitutional rule. Here is a selection of them:</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768392/original/file-20261026-52-m0yll3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man at a desk, gesturing with his hands." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768392/original/file-20261026-52-m0yll3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768392/original/file-20261026-52-m0yll3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768392/original/file-20261026-52-m0yll3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768392/original/file-20261026-52-m0yll3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768392/original/file-20261026-52-m0yll3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768392/original/file-20261026-52-m0yll3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768392/original/file-20261026-52-m0yll3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<h2>1. The Constitution bars presidential control</h2>

<p>“States are empowered under <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/article-1/section-4/">Article 1, Section 4, of the Constitution</a> to conduct elections and set the time, place and manner of those elections,” former federal judge John E. Jones told The Conversation in an interview on April 22, 2026. Jones was discussing Trump’s <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/03/ensuring-citizenship-verification-and-integrity-in-federal-elections/">March 31 executive order</a> to take control of mail-in voting from states and give it to the U.S. Postal Service and the Department of Homeland Security. </p>

<p>Jones, who is now the president of Dickinson College, explained why the framers of the Constitution set up a process in which states run elections and not the federal government:</p>

<p>“First of all, the federal government didn’t have the apparatus to conduct elections. And states had been running elections; they knew how to do it. There was a great deal of trust in the states’ ability to run elections. And there was the core debate of federalism, as to what powers states could retain, and they didn’t want to abdicate many of those powers,” Jones said. </p>

<p>There was also, Jones added, “a debate about the potential for fraud, that if there was a single entity controlling all the elections – that is, if you centralize elections under one politically motivated executive – it’s a really fraught situation which can be abused.” </p>

<p>“The Constitution is clear,” said Jones. “Unless amended, Article 1, Section 4 is – to use the trite phrase – what it is. The power rests with the states, absent congressional action. There is no mention of the president. None.”</p>

<h2>2. Limits on Congress, too</h2>

<p>The Republican-controlled House also tried this year to horn in on the constitutional power of states to regulate elections and who can vote. </p>

<p>In February 2026, the House, urged by Trump, <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/7296">passed the SAVE America Act</a>. The act would have required those registering to vote in federal elections to – in person – “provide documentary proof of U.S. citizenship.” It also required some people who were voting in federal elections to give proof of U.S. citizenship.</p>

<p>John J. Martin, an election law scholar at Quinnipiac University Law School, wrote that the act “presents a constitutional dilemma. By requiring individuals to show documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to vote, the SAVE America Act is implicitly saying that someone must be a U.S. citizen to vote in federal elections.”</p>

<p>In other words, Martin wrote, “Congress would be instituting a qualification to vote, a power that the Constitution leaves exclusively to the states. Normally, when state and federal laws conflict, <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artVI-C2-1/ALDE_00013395/">the Constitution’s supremacy clause</a> mandates that federal law prevails. Yet, in this instance, where Congress has no actual authority to implement voter qualifications, the SAVE America Act would seem to have no constitutional leg on which to stand.” </p>

<p>The Senate proved unwilling to pass the SAVE Act this year, so this particular constitutional battle has yet to hit the courts.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Trump frequently targets <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/voters-trust-local-election-officials-theyre-less-sure-about-the-mail">mail voting, claiming it’s rife with fraud</a>. The <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/executive-order-14399-ensuring-citizenship-verification-and-integrity-federal-elections">March 2026 executive order</a> by the president aimed, it said, to ensure “integrity in federal elections” by placing severe restrictions on mail voting.</p>

<p>Among that order’s provisions was a directive to the U.S. Postal Service to implement, election scholar Martin wrote, “uniform ballot and envelope requirements for mail and absentee ballots used in federal elections.” The order also mandated that states must “provide the Postal Service, 60 days prior to Election Day, with lists of all voters eligible to vote by mail or absentee.”  </p>

<p>A mail ballot that didn’t comply with the Postal Service’s requirements, or was sent by somebody not on a state-provided list, would not be delivered by the Postal Service, wrote Martin, “effectively canceling that vote.”</p>

<p>Lawsuits were filed by a host of state officials and voting rights groups. The suits eventually made their way up to the U.S. Supreme Court. </p>

<p>Martin summarized their arguments: “The president does not possess unilateral authority to alter the methods of voting in federal elections. Rather, the <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/article-1/section-4/clause-1/">elections clause</a> of the Constitution vests the authority to regulate the ‘time, place, and manner’ of federal elections in the states. Congress also has the authority to regulate federal elections, if it chooses to do so.”</p>

<p>On Sept. 14, 2026, the Supreme Court apparently agreed, with a <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/26a305_4g15.pdf#page=2">7-2 vote upholding a preliminary injunction</a> blocking the new rules.</p>

<title>How Lula turned the tables on the right in Brazil and the US with his comeback presidential victory</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768308/original/file-20261026-52-ahzwjv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1023%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva addresses supporters during a victory rally in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on Oct. 25, 2026, after winning a fourth presidential term.
</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/APTOPIX%20Brazil%20Election/2d47b97acf584914b6f598e8b5561a98/photo">AP Photo/Natacha Pisarenko</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A leader who stood up to U.S. President Donald Trump just won an election in Latin America’s biggest country, reversing a <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2026/10/24/latin-americas-maga-wave-is-widening-trumps-political-military-reach/">trend of new right-wing governments</a> in the region over the past two years.</p>

<p>Incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/06/keeping-up-with-the-bolsonaros-flavios-surprise-first-round-election-win-heralds-rise-of-a-political-dynasty">having narrowly lost</a> to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of voting on Oct. 5, 2026, staged a remarkable comeback on Oct. 25. He erased the deficit and won the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-interactive/2026/oct/25/brazil-election-2026-live-second-round-results">all-important runoff election</a> by more than 3.5 percentage points – more than 4 million votes.</p>

<p>It was a stunning result for the leader who proved to be the first Brazilian candidate to win a presidential election after not winning the first round, and who had been all but written off for a possible win. As a <a href="https://stonecenter.tulane.edu/anthony-w-pereira">professor of Latin American politics</a>, I believe the result offers a number of key political lessons for Brazil, Latin America – and even the United States.</p>

<h2>A contest of worldviews — and social media</h2>

<p>The choice in the second-round election was stark. Lula offered measures to ameliorate steep income inequalities and an economy built on a transition to clean energy, environmental protection and increased access to higher education and technical training. On international matters, Lula balanced defending Brazilian sovereignty from a Trump administration <a href="https://theconversation.com/trumps-coercive-tactics-in-latin-america-evoke-era-of-gunboat-diplomacy-and-the-rise-of-anti-imperialism-it-helped-spur-279238">keen on meddling in Latin America</a>, and maintaining good relations with an array of nations and blocs, including the European Union and China.</p>

<p>Bolsonaro, meanwhile, promised sweeping cuts to government spending, more militarized policing and eager support for the Trump administration’s <a href="https://theconversation.com/trumps-narco-terrorism-war-in-latin-america-evokes-reagan-then-as-now-its-more-about-fighting-leftists-than-drug-runners-284287">campaign against drug violence</a>. His pitch also came with offers to U.S. investors <a href="https://atlasinstitute.org/flavio-bolsonaros-washington-visit-highlights-security-minerals-and-diplomatic-tensions-between-brazil-and-the-us/">of access to critical minerals</a> in Brazil. </p>

<p>Such right-wing populism has been ascendant in Latin America of late, and Lula also had to overcome an anti-incumbent mood, brought on by high prices, stagnant salaries, steep interest rates and a <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/how-an-obscure-banker-slipped-into-brazils-political-inner-circle-triggering-2026-03-13/">massive corruption scandal</a> involving Brazilian elites. That banking probe directly <a href="https://www.intercept.com.br/2026/05/13/audio-flavio-negociou-vorcaro-milhoes/">ensnared Bolsonaro himself</a>, as well as powerful Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes, whom Bolsonaro’s supporters <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/13/scandal-brazil-court-jair-flavio-bolsonaro-power-election-moraes-lula">had tried to link</a> to Lula. </p>

<p>Lula also had to neuter a social media landscape that has been <a href="https://apublica.org/sentinela/2022/10/no-2o-turno-bolsonaro-aposta-em-fake-news-que-liga-lula-ao-crime-organizado/">dominated by images</a> and <a href="https://veja.abril.com.br/politica/tse-manda-flavio-e-apoiadores-excluirem-videos-falsos-de-uso-de-drogas-em-ato-pro-lula/">narratives</a> disparaging the president and his Workers’ Party. </p>

<p>Right-wing <a href="https://www.meioemensagem.com.br/marketing/eleicao-de-bolsonaro-marca-mudanca-no-marketing-politico">dominance of that online ecosystem</a> <a href="https://www.scielo.br/j/rbcpol/a/TsmbKCcpgQW8dRWLNd8vfZR/abstract/?lang=pt">helped carry</a> Jair Bolsonaro, the 2026 hopeful’s father, to power in 2018 and got him close to reelection in 2022.</p>

<p>Especially after the first-round results in the 2026 vote, many analysts assumed the same <a href="https://g1.globo.com/politica/eleicoes/2026/noticia/2026/10/09/disputa-digital-lula-reune-jovens-influenciadores-eleitos-e-aliados-de-flavio-organizam-reacao-nas-redes.ghtml">pro-Bolsonaro social media presence</a> would once again be hegemonic. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Two men embrace." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768380/original/file-20261026-52-mv84h6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768380/original/file-20261026-52-mv84h6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768380/original/file-20261026-52-mv84h6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768380/original/file-20261026-52-mv84h6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768380/original/file-20261026-52-mv84h6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768380/original/file-20261026-52-mv84h6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768380/original/file-20261026-52-mv84h6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Brazilian lawmaker André Janones embraces President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as he delivers a victory speech after winning a fourth term in the presidential runoff on Oct. 25, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/APTOPIX%20Brazil%20Election/d441d5331ede43828387a2f5bf669fa7/photo">AP Photo/Andre Penner</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Instead, after the first round, a network of young, tech-savvy pro-Lula communicators created and shared effective, often amusing videos on WhatsApp and Instagram. </p>

<p>And they appealed to the center and even some of the right. All told, Lula easily made up more than 2 million votes by which he lost in the first round. He didn’t just increase turnout by millions and lower abstention rates; he also saw the state with the country’s second-largest electorate, Minas Gerais, <a href="https://edition.cnn.com/2026/10/26/americas/brazil-election-results-takeaways-latam-hk-intl">flip to his side entirely</a> – a swing of nearly 700,000 votes.</p>

<p>Emblematic of the strength of the campaign was the growth in subscribers to the <a href="https://www.bbc.com/portuguese/articles/c678pegn3krmo">WhatsApp channel Lula’s Army</a>, which grew from 50,000 on Oct. 5 to more than 10 million by the night of the historic election.</p>

<p>The creator of the channel, André Janones, is a federal deputy for the Rede Party, an ally of the Workers’ Party, and a rising star in the circle around Lula. Likewise, Ana Elisa Santos Silva, a 21-year-old <a href="https://g1.globo.com/mg/centro-oeste/eleicoes/2026/noticia/2026/10/05/quem-e-ana-elisa-influenciadora-eleita-deputada-mais-jovem-de-mg.ghtml">digital influencer and law student</a> in the Workers’ Party, got the most votes of any federal deputy in the swing state of Minas Gerais.</p>

<h2>Cracks in the ‘Americanization’ theory of politics</h2>

<p>A prevalent narrative of Brazilian politics has held that the country’s divisions increasingly mirror those of the United States. </p>

<p>Part of that idea is due to Trump’s loss in the 2020 election and the resulting attack on the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, which <a href="https://korbel.du.edu/resource/how-us-capitol-insurrection-influenced-jan-8-violence-in-brazil/">eerily presaged events</a> following Jair Bolsanaro’s 2022 loss. </p>

<p>Like in the U.S., there has also been a rapid rise of a <a href="https://aeon.co/essays/what-will-an-evangelical-brazil-look-like">politically active evangelical right</a> in Brazil.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A large crowd of demonstrators march with flags and other banners." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768379/original/file-20261026-62-1wjjrw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768379/original/file-20261026-62-1wjjrw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768379/original/file-20261026-62-1wjjrw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768379/original/file-20261026-62-1wjjrw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768379/original/file-20261026-62-1wjjrw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768379/original/file-20261026-62-1wjjrw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768379/original/file-20261026-62-1wjjrw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
