            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>More fundamentally, proponents of the <a href="https://bahiaeconomica.com.br/economia-e-politica/sonho-do-proprio-negocio-atinge-41-dos-brasileiros-209776">Americanization thesis</a> hold that U.S.-style deindustrialization and “Uberization” of the Brazilian economy have led to a decline of the unionized working class – a core support base for the left – and its replacement by an army of gig employees <a href="https://tribunademinas.com.br/maistendencias/ter-o-proprio-negocio-ou-garantir-os-direitos-da-carteira-assinada-pesquisa-revela-qual-caminho-os-brasileiros-mais-associam-a-uma-vida-melhor#goog_rewarded">dreaming of owning their own businesses</a> and throwing off the shackles of the taxing and regulating state.</p>

<p>Yet similarities between the two countries shouldn’t be confused for politics always moving on parallel tracks. </p>

<p>Survey <a href="https://iclnoticias.com.br/economia/maioria-brasileiros-estado-ipsos/">research suggests</a> that many Brazilians see the <a href="https://multivix.edu.br/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/o-estado-como-garantidor-dos-direitos-sociais.pdf">state as responsible</a> for the realization of their constitutionally protected social rights, including healthcare, education and pensions. Many also regard government employment as inherently more stable and dignified than the harsh labor markets of the private sector, especially for the relatively unskilled. </p>

<p>For all of the apparent rise in American-style libertarian politics in Brazil, the reality is that such a viewpoint remains much smaller in the country. Flávio Bolsonaro’s bet, like his father’s before him, was that this strain of libertarian right-wing politics could nonetheless propel him to victory, <a href="https://ffms.pt/pt-pt/atualmentes/argentina-elegeu-o-primeiro-presidente-liberal-libertario-da-historia-da-humanidade">much as it apparently had for Javier Milei</a> in Argentina in 2023. But it was not enough.</p>

<h2>One election can’t fix deep polarization</h2>

<p>Even with Lula’s win, Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party did exceptionally well at the legislative level. </p>

<p>When the next Brazilian Congress convenes on Feb. 1, 2027, the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/right-wing-wave-brazils-congress-boosts-bolsonaro-camp-ahead-presidential-runoff-2026-10-05/">Liberal Party will control</a> 28 seats in the Senate  – 35% of the total; and 121 seats in the lower house – 24% of the total (as well as five governorships, which are 19% of the total). </p>

<p>When factoring in expected Liberal Party allies, it is clear that the right will have bigger majorities in both houses for Lula’s next administration. That will help <a href="https://sumauma.com/por-que-o-congresso-ganhou-tanto-poder-e-por-que-isso-torna-mais-dificil-renova-lo/">Congress solidify</a> control vis-a-vis the executive branch in terms of legislation and, crucially, the budget. </p>

<h2>A series of unknowns facing Lula</h2>

<p>The election raises several questions.</p>

<p>First, it is unclear how Lula, who will turn 81 on Oct. 27, will be able to effectively govern. The president will have to make major concessions to a Congress with little capacity for responsibly delivering coherent policy.</p>

<p>The federal Supreme Court is also seen as politicized, fragmented and tainted by scandals. On the other hand, Lula <a href="https://g1.globo.com/politica/noticia/2026/10/26/reeleito-lula-pode-indicar-mais-4-ministros-para-o-stf-no-proximo-mandato.ghtml">could appoint</a> four new Supreme Court justices because of upcoming retirements, meaning that he could shape the country’s highest judicial body in a way that enhances his ability to manage Congress.</p>



<p>Yet it might be difficult for Lula to simultaneously meet the demands coming from Congress and those from the business community. For example, many will push the government to curb the fiscal deficit, currently running at a <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/bffe028e-838d-4e74-b05e-62f6db4978db?syn-25a6b1a6=1">very high annual level</a> of close to 8% of gross domestic product. </p>

<p>A second question is whether Bolsonaro’s loss will splinter the right. One interpretation of the 2026 election is that to be competitive, the right will want to move on from the Bolsonaro family. One potential figure is Tarcísio de Freitas, a former cabinet member in the Jair Bolsonaro government and popular governor of São Paulo. Yet there are nonetheless five members of the Bolsonaro family in the new Congress, and they are likely to try to keep together the coalition that fought for Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign.</p>

<p>Finally, it’s not clear how the Trump administration, which <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/sep/01/us-trump-rubio-meddling-brazil-election">interfered decisively against Lula’s agenda</a>, will react to his win – and to what extent it will support Bolsonaro’s denial of his election loss even though it was bigger than his father’s in 2022. </p>

<p>Whatever the extent of any interference, the Trump administration’s right-wing Latin American vision invariably sets up conflict with Lula. Yet while the Trump preference was always for Flávio Bolsonaro, that doesn’t mean his administration won’t pragmatically engage with Lula <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-a-diplomatic-snub-evokes-the-complicated-us-brazil-relationship-in-the-second-trump-era-278649">even as it pressures</a> his government. For his part, Lula continues to hold his own leverage, including through Brazil’s <a href="https://www.bbc.com/portuguese/articles/cglpyzegwkko">large deposits of rare earth elements</a> that the Trump administration covets.</p>

<p>If the past eight years of Brazilian politics are any guide, Lula’s next administration is likely to be a turbulent one in which enduring <a href="https://cebri.org/br/midia/710/riscos-globais-em-2026-e-implicacoes-para-o-posicionamento-estrategico-do-brasil">divisions at home and abroad</a> are continually tested.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294810/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Anthony W. Pereira has received research funding from FAPESP, the Sao Paulo research council, and the British Academy. He is a senior fellow of Canning House, a think tank focused on Latin America and Iberia. </span></em></p></content>

<title>Ghost stories don’t just scare us – they remind us of historical injustices</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767312/original/file-20261020-50-dbv7np.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5700%2C3800&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">What makes a ghost story unforgettable?</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/female-ghost-looking-through-glass-window-of-royalty-free-image/1707507933?phrase=haunted&amp;adppopup=true">Maskot/Maskot via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Along with the pumpkins and costumes, the candles and cobwebs, Halloween is all about storytelling. From tales of haunted houses to accounts of demonic possession, ghost stories are part of the holiday’s appeal.  </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://machias.edu/people/marcus-librizzi/">professor at the University of Maine who specializes</a> in ghost stories, I’ve thought a lot about what makes one unforgettable. My <a href="https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Haunted-Islands-in-the-Gulf-of-Maine/Marcus-LiBrizzi/9781608936373">field research</a> has taken me from the coast of Maine to the Amazon jungle, but some factors remain constant in an unforgettable tale.  </p>

<p>One factor is what I call “creep value,” which includes the scare factor but also the elements of a story that might be simply unsettling or uncanny. </p>

<p>Take, for starters, the ghost of Catherine’s Hill along the Blacks Woods Road in Maine. The story warns that, against all intuition, even a lone driver at night must always stop and <a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/Dark_Woods_Chill_Waters/CnoYAwAAQBAJ?hl=en&amp;gbpv=1&amp;dq=dark+woods+chill+waters&amp;printsec=frontcover">offer the phantom woman a ride</a>. If not, as the story goes, she will appear when least expected in the back seat of the car to cause a fatal accident. </p>

<p>But there is more to account for than creep value in an unforgettable ghost story. These stories can keep alive the memory of a dark past. In my research I have come across tales that preserve memories of injustices that might otherwise have been forgotten.</p>

<h2>Dark histories</h2>

<p>One story, about a ghost ship that can be heard but never seen, preserves the little-known history of the smuggling of enslaved people. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768306/original/file-20261026-62-41gr9f.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black and white photograph showing a full moon and its reflection in a body of water with silhouettes of trees along the shore." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768306/original/file-20261026-62-41gr9f.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768306/original/file-20261026-62-41gr9f.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768306/original/file-20261026-62-41gr9f.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768306/original/file-20261026-62-41gr9f.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768306/original/file-20261026-62-41gr9f.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768306/original/file-20261026-62-41gr9f.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768306/original/file-20261026-62-41gr9f.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A full moon over Seal Harbor.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Marcus Librizzi</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The legend goes that on foggy nights, during the full moon, those standing at the Cooksey Drive Overlook in Seal Harbor, just outside Acadia National Park, can hear the slaves in the hold of a <a href="https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Ghosts-of-Acadia/Marcus-LiBrizzi/9780892729210">sinking ship</a> crying for help. </p>

<p>The story goes back to the <a href="https://newspaperarchive.com/bar-harbor-mount-desert-herald-jun-21-1883-p-1/">Pride of the Seas</a>, a ship that smuggled enslaved Africans into the United States after the trans-Atlantic slave trade had been abolished but slavery remained legal. The account specifies that the smugglers scuttled the ship to evade the law. In ghost stories that circulate by word of mouth on Mount Desert Island, the screams of those left behind can still be heard.</p>

<p>Pennsylvania coal miners offer another example of past grievances passed down in the form of ghost stories. At the sites of deadly accidents, people have reported the sound of a pickaxe or the groans of a dying man. An <a href="https://wynninghistory.com/2025/10/01/ghost-stories-and-dark-folklore-korson/">extensive archive</a> contains multiple accounts of coal miners witnessing ghostly knocking, disembodied voices and apparitions of mangled men. One story involves an innocent coal miner, condemned to death in 1877, who left a <a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/Pennsylvania/bfaultPxl18C?hl=en&amp;gbpv=1&amp;dq=story+of+handprint+from+coal+miner+that+will+never+go+away&amp;pg=PA79&amp;printsec=frontcover">handprint in his cell</a> at the Carbon County Jail that no amount of sanding or paint has been able to erase. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768253/original/file-20261026-52-eeukz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An engraving depicting miners using picks and shovels." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768253/original/file-20261026-52-eeukz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768253/original/file-20261026-52-eeukz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=381&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768253/original/file-20261026-52-eeukz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=381&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768253/original/file-20261026-52-eeukz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=381&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768253/original/file-20261026-52-eeukz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=478&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768253/original/file-20261026-52-eeukz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=478&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768253/original/file-20261026-52-eeukz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=478&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Coal miners endured brutal work conditions in the 19th and 20th centuries.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/anthracite-coal-mine-pennsylvania-royalty-free-illustration/2170518933?phrase=pennsylvania%20coal%20miners&amp;adppopup=true">ilbusca/DigitalVision Vectors via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Today, it is widely known that coal miners of the 19th and early 20th centuries experienced ruthless exploitation and hazardous working conditions. Years ago, their <a href="https://www.kentuckypress.com/9780813191041/pennsylvania-mining-families/">plight went unrecognized</a> in official histories and government policies, but ghost stories helped keep these experiences in the collective memory.</p>

<h2>A South American perspective</h2>

<p>When I collected ghost stories in South America, the same pattern held true: Some tales preserved history that would otherwise be lost. </p>

<p>In the Amazon jungle of northern Brazil, I traveled to a gloomy site where people, over several generations, have claimed to see the spirits of young men in the murky water. These stories keep alive injustices from the 19th century involving <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/26394962">enslavement of Indigenous people</a>. The location was a former sugarcane plantation notorious for cruelty, and accounts of apparitions in the water are a reminder of this history. </p>

<p>In Rio de Janeiro a well-known ghost story involves the apparition of a young girl in a mansion known as the <a href="http://www.rememberio.org/post/flamengo-castle">Castelinho do Flamengo</a>. All the accounts of her story agree that this young heiress, named Maria de Lourdes Fernandes, witnessed the deaths of her parents; her guardian then locked her up and drove her to suicide to get her inheritance. </p>

<p>Her soul is said to remain in the mansion she tried to escape. The tale is not just about an individual tragedy but one that exposes inequities involving the mistreatment of juveniles and the corrupting influence of power.</p>

<h2>The past that isn’t past</h2>

<p>Ghost stories don’t simply recount memories – they can revive them and bring the past back into the present.</p>

<p>The unsolved 1898 murder of a 52-year-old woman, Sarah Ware, in Bucksport, Maine, illustrates how ghost stories can have historical significance and flood the present with the past.</p>

<p>In the 1980s a woman and her daughter began having nightmares about a long-haired woman in a long dress struggling to rise from the bottom of a lake. When they realized they were having the same <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1065906/">recurring dream</a>, they partnered with an author, and their research led them to a conclusion that the apparition was the ghost of Ware. </p>

<p>Official records document that when Ware’s body was recovered it was badly decomposed and her <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dTZcUYSmwWY">head had completely detached</a>. Her head remained in the courthouse until the 1990s, when it was buried in Ware’s grave. According to local lore, however, Ware’s headless body is not in that grave but instead in her original grave, now located at the bottom of Silver Lake. In the oral history of the area, workers moved only the tombstones when they flooded the paupers’ graveyard – the cemetery for the poor – to make a reservoir in the 1930s.</p>

<p>Ware’s ghost is believed to have appeared again in 2006. When a young woman went scuba diving in <a href="https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Ghosts-of-Acadia/Marcus-LiBrizzi/9780892729210">Silver Lake</a> in Bucksport, she reported seeing a woman in a long dress struggling to rise from the bottom of the lake. When she swam over to help, the figure’s hair floated back with the movement of the water to reveal she was a faceless apparition. The sighting of the faceless ghost revived the history of the unsolved murder all over again. </p>

<p>Ware’s case highlights the violence and injustice and their connection to gender and social class in 19th-century Maine. Missing evidence and recanted testimonies suggest that powerful men might have <a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/In_Search_of_Sarah_Ware/r1RRR3j20EYC?hl=en&amp;gbpv=0">interfered with the investigation</a> to hide their own complicity in the murder. As an independent woman of the time, Ware was the subject of gossip, and the treatment of her body shows how social class affects even the honoring of the dead. As a ghost story, the history of Sarah Ware is not past but rather part of the here and now. </p>

<p>So when you’re out and about telling ghost stories this Halloween, remember that the unforgettable ones are all about creep value in the context of a dark history that flows back in again like the tide.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293080/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: If Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts can get dangerous blood clots, so can you – here’s how some states are trying to reduce the risk

<title>If Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts can get dangerous blood clots, so can you – here’s how some states are trying to reduce the risk</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767986/original/file-20261023-50-qmx2qh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8640%2C5760&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season after a blood clot in his leg traveled to both lungs.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/philadelphia-eagles-quarterback-jalen-hurts-looks-on-during-news-photo/2298509324">Andy Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Jalen Hurts is 28, a Super Bowl MVP and an elite athlete in peak physical condition. He was also recently diagnosed with <a href="https://abcnews.com/GMA/Culture/eagles-qb-jalen-hurts-sidelined-blood-clots-timeline/story?id=137409068">blood clots in his leg and both lungs</a>. </p>

<p>After a cleat to the left calf during a game against the Los Angeles Rams on Oct. 4, 2026, and after a team flight to London, the Philadelphia Eagles quarterback was given an ultrasound and diagnosed with a superficial vein thrombosis, which is a blood clot in the vein near the skin, in his left leg.</p>

<p>He played that Sunday. A follow-up ultrasound showed the superficial vein clot had progressed to a deeper vein, and he was diagnosed with a deep vein thrombosis, or DVT.</p>

<p>By Oct. 19, he was diagnosed with a bilateral pulmonary embolism, which means he had blood clots in both lungs. He started treatment with blood thinners, and his prognosis was described as “very good,” according to a <a href="https://www.instagram.com/philadelphiaeagles/p/DercP9xRobx/?hl=en">statement from the team and his agent</a>, but he will likely be <a href="https://www.nfl.com/news/eagles-qb-jalen-hurts-out-2026-season-blood-clots">out for the rest of the season</a>. </p>

<p>For me, as a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Hje7W2kAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">pulmonary vascular disease specialist</a> who treats patients with blood clots and pulmonary embolisms, this case highlights an important teaching moment. If this can happen to an elite athlete, it can happen to anyone. And too often, it can be prevented. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ZrYeirUL2SE?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">ESPN reports on the “shocking” news about Jalen Hurts.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>3 major risk factors</h2>

<p>Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism are grouped under one name: <a href="https://www.health.harvard.edu/a_to_z/thromboembolism-deep-vein-thrombosis-and-pulmonary-embolism-a-to-z">venous thromboembolism</a>.</p>

<p>When a deep vein thrombosis develops, the <a href="https://www.health.harvard.edu/a_to_z/thromboembolism-deep-vein-thrombosis-and-pulmonary-embolism-a-to-z">clot can break off</a> and a piece of it can travel through the body and lodge in the arteries in the lungs, where it obstructs blood flow and lowers oxygen in the blood, causing shortness of breath and strain on the heart. This is known as <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/pulmonary-embolism/symptoms-causes/syc-20354647">pulmonary embolism</a>. If the blood clot in the lungs is large enough, it can sometimes kill within hours.</p>

<p>Clots that happen near the skin, like the one first found in Hurts’ leg, are often treated as minor but are not always harmless. It is estimated that a <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1590/1677-5449.180105">quarter of people diagnosed with superficial clots</a> can also have deep vein thrombosis, so health providers order follow-up imaging. </p>

<p>In the United States, <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/blood-clots/data-research/facts-stats/index.html">up to 900,000 people</a> are affected by venous thromboembolism each year. An estimated 60,000 to 100,000 die from it annually. Survivors often have long-term symptoms such as persistent leg swelling, shortness of breath, chronic clots, or elevated blood pressure in the arteries in the lungs, which is known as <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17635-chronic-thromboembolic-pulmonary-hypertension-cteph">chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension</a>.</p>

<p>The three main factors that drive formation of blood clots are injury to the vein wall, slow or stagnant blood flow in that injured region, and blood that clots easily due to inflammation or other factors. This is called Virchow’s triad, and Hurts’ story touches every corner of this triad. </p>

<p>The injury to the left calf bruised the muscle and likely the vein beneath it. Later, prolonged sitting on an overnight flight from Philadelphia to London and a return flight after the game resulted in stagnant blood flow to the injured leg. Inflammation from the injury along with dehydration from the game and jet lag all may have contributed to increased blood clotting. </p>

<h2>Florida’s first-in-the-nation law</h2>

<p>Beyond Hurts’ case, the <a href="https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/venous-thromboembolism/causes">most common risk factors</a> to developing venous thromboembolism include hospitalization and surgery, especially orthopedic surgery and abdominal operations.</p>

<p>More than a third of cases occur <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/blood-clots/data-research/facts-stats/index.html">following a hospital admission</a> or just after discharge. Fractures and blunt trauma to the legs, prolonged immobility or bed rest, having a leg in a cast, or sitting for hours in a plane or car all predispose to blood clot formation in the legs. The use of estrogen in birth control pills or hormone therapy, cancer, pregnancy and inherited clotting disorders also predispose an otherwise healthy person to develop blood clots. </p>

<p>It is estimated that <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/blood-clots/risk-factors/ha-vte.html">up to 70% of hospital-associated clots can be avoided</a> with prophylactic blood thinners or inflatable leg devices called sequential compression devices to prevent deep vein thrombosis. However, fewer than half of hospital patients receive such measures, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. </p>

<p>For people taking long trips in a car or plane, it is recommended to take frequent movement breaks, stay hydrated and even use compression socks. New symptoms of calf swelling, tenderness or redness should raise concerns for possible deep vein thrombosis.</p>

<p>Hurts had elite doctors and close monitoring, so his clots were caught and treated quickly. Most individuals do not have the same protections. </p>

<p>In 2025, Florida was the first state in the country to pass a law to help identify and treat those at risk of blood clots. It’s called the <a href="https://flhouse.gov/Sections/Bills/billsdetail.aspx?BillId=82134">Emily Adkins Family Protection Act</a>. Adkins tragically passed away in 2022 at age 23 from a fatal pulmonary embolism that occurred after a clot from her leg traveled to her lungs. Her family helped pass the bill that set up the nation’s first state <a href="https://www.fhca.org/media_center/entry/florida_legislature_passes_emily_adkins_family_protection_act">blood clot and pulmonary embolism work group</a>, which put forward the recommendations that later turned into law. </p>

<p>Florida’s law requires hospitals to have protocols to assess and treat patients at risk of blood clots and train hospital staff to recognize the symptoms of venous thromboembolism. It also will involve the creation of a statewide venous thromboembolism registry, the first of its kind in the country, where hospitals will report data on blood clots.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ejnBuX0HbMs?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A 2025 Florida law mandates every healthcare facility in the state to have an action plan for diagnosing, treating and preventing blood clots.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Florida is no longer alone. In 2026, the <a href="https://www.stoptheclot.org/news/update-april-28-2026-blake-burgess-blood-clot-prevention-act-passes-senate/">Blake Burgess Blood Clot Prevention Act</a> was passed in Oklahoma; <a href="https://www.stoptheclot.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Mississippi-Legislation.pdf">Mississippi</a> proposed similar legislation. Advocates such as the National Blood Clot Alliance are <a href="https://www.stoptheclot.org/news/nbca-urges-national-action/">urging other states to follow</a>. </p>

<p>Hurts will most likely recover over the next few months. The outcome for many other individuals will depend on whether someone asks the right questions, recognizes the warning signs and acts in time. Venous thromboembolism is one of the few major killers where risk assessment, prevention, early diagnosis and fast treatment can play a critical role in changing the outcome. </p>

<title>Why do people still get polio in some countries and not in others?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765681/original/file-20261012-50-fqledy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6719%2C4479&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">In Pakistan, where wild polio still has not been eliminated, health workers go door to door vaccinating young children.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/healthcare-worker-administers-polio-drops-to-a-child-for-news-photo/2276509559?phrase=vaccinating%20kids%20against%20polio%20pakistan&amp;adppopup=true">ARIF ALI/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure>

<p><em><a href="https://theconversation.com/us/topics/curious-kids-us-74795">Curious Kids</a> is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to <a href="mailto:curiouskidsus@theconversation.com">CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com</a>.</em></p>

<hr>

<blockquote>
<p><strong>Why are people still getting polio in some countries and in not others? – Mia, age 9, Centennial, Colorado</strong></p>
</blockquote>

<hr>

<p>On a busy street in Karachi, Pakistan, a healthcare worker kneels down so she’s eye to eye with a toddler. She squeezes two drops of liquid onto the child’s tongue. Then she takes out a purple marker and colors the child’s pinkie fingernail so everyone can see that this toddler is now vaccinated against polio.</p>

<p>During big vaccination drives, thousands of health workers like her knock on doors across Pakistan.</p>

<p>Most kids in the United States will never experience anything like this, because they get the polio vaccine as a shot at the doctor’s office instead of drops in a door-to-door campaign.</p>

<p>The two vaccines <a href="https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/polio-vaccine.html">work a little differently</a>, but both protect kids from the polio virus. The countries that still see polio outbreaks are places where not enough people have gotten the preventive vaccine.</p>

<p><a href="https://publichealth.uic.edu/profiles/wallace-katrine/">I’m an epidemiologist</a> – a scientist who studies how diseases spread. My work focuses on diseases that vaccines can prevent, and on the false information that keeps some families from getting those vaccines.</p>

<h2>A sneaky virus</h2>

<p>Polio is <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/poliomyelitis">caused by a virus</a> that lives in the human gut. It spreads when tiny bits of poop from an infected person get onto hands, food or water, and then into someone else’s mouth. That’s why polio spreads fastest in places without clean water or good sewer systems.</p>

<p>Polio is sneaky. Most people who catch it <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/polio/factsheet/index.html">never feel sick at all</a>, so they can pass it on without knowing.</p>

<p>But in about <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/poliomyelitis">1 out of every 200</a> infections globally, the virus attacks the nerves that control muscles, usually in the legs. This can cause a person to be paralyzed for the rest of their life.</p>

<p>There is no cure for polio. But there is a <a href="https://www.who.int/teams/immunization-vaccines-and-biologicals/diseases/poliomyelitis-(polio)">vaccine</a>, and a few doses can protect you for life.</p>

<h2>How vaccines pushed polio back</h2>

<p>In 1988, polio <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/mm7034a1.htm">paralyzed about 350,000 children</a> in 125 countries. That same year, <a href="https://polioeradication.org/who-we-are/">countries around the world teamed up</a> with one huge goal: Wipe out polio for good.</p>

<p>Though polio has not yet been entirely eliminated, this effort has been a major success. Since then, polio cases have <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/global-polio-vaccination/about/index.html">dropped by more than 99% globally</a>. </p>

<p>There used to be <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/poliomyelitis">three types of wild polio virus</a>. Now, <a href="https://www.who.int/health-topics/poliomyelitis#tab=tab_1">only type 1</a> is left.</p>

<p><iframe id="eeUMZ" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/eeUMZ/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="map of the world showing countries where polio has been found in sewage, where wild polio spread and where vaccine-derived polio spread in 2025"></iframe></p>

<h2>Where wild polio still hides</h2>

<p>Wild polio, the original virus, now spreads in <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/feature-stories/detail/pakistan-and-afghanistan-the-final-wild-poliovirus-bastion">just two countries</a>: Afghanistan and Pakistan. In 2025, wild polio paralyzed <a href="https://polioeradication.org/about-polio/polio-this-week/">52 children</a> there.</p>

<p>Both countries have <a href="https://theconversation.com/calculating-the-costs-of-the-afghanistan-war-in-lives-dollars-and-years-164588">lived through</a> <a href="https://theconversation.com/india-pakistan-strikes-5-essential-reads-on-decades-of-rivalry-and-tensions-over-kashmir-256157">decades of war</a>. In some areas, it’s too dangerous for vaccinators to travel, and some have even <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/two-killed-attack-pakistani-polio-vaccination-team-2024-09-11/">been attacked</a>.</p>

<p>In Afghanistan, vaccinators haven’t gone house to house <a href="https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2026-statement-of-the-forty-fourth-meeting-of-the-polio-ihr-emergency-committee">since late 2024</a>. Families must bring children to central spots, such as mosques, instead. But the kids who can’t get there miss their vaccines.</p>

<h2>When too few kids are vaccinated</h2>

<p>Some countries have outbreaks of a different kind, called <a href="https://doi.org/10.53854/liim-3102-5">vaccine-derived polio</a>.</p>

<p>The oral polio vaccine, which is no longer used in many countries, including the U.S., contains a weakened polio virus – too weak to make a child sick, but strong enough to teach the body to fight polio.</p>

<p>After a child swallows the drops of vaccine, some of the weakened virus leaves their body in their poop. If nearly every kid around is vaccinated, the virus has nowhere to go and fizzles out.</p>

<p>But in areas where <a href="https://historyofvaccines.org/vaccines-101/what-do-vaccines-do/how-herd-immunity-works/">fewer than 80% of kids</a> are vaccinated, it can pass from child to child. Like a message in a game of telephone, the virus changes a little each time it’s passed. Eventually, it can change back into a form that paralyzes children.</p>

<p>That might sound like the vaccine is the problem. But in fact, the problem is that too few kids have received the vaccine.</p>

<p>The children who go unvaccinated are usually the hardest to reach: kids in the poorest families, in faraway villages or in war zones. In one study in Pakistan, offering families other free healthcare along with polio drops cuts the share of never-vaccinated kids <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/vaccines12121340">nearly in half</a>.</p>

<h2>The polio that went nowhere</h2>

<p>In October 2025, scientists testing sewage in Hamburg, Germany, <a href="https://polioeradication.org/news/detection-of-wild-poliovirus-type-1-wpv1-in-environmental-sample-in-germany/">found wild polio</a>. Its genes matched virus found in Afghanistan, more than 3,000 miles (4,800 kilometers) away.</p>

<p>This means that someone carrying the virus, probably without feeling sick, had traveled to Germany. But not a single child there was paralyzed because most German kids are vaccinated against polio.</p>

<p>Other countries in Europe found vaccine-derived polio in their sewage in 2025, with the same happy ending.</p>

<p>Polio can travel anywhere, but it can only hurt kids where they aren’t protected by the vaccine.</p>

<h2>When rumors stop vaccines</h2>

<p>Polio also gets help spreading from rumors and misinformation. In 2003, false stories that the vaccine was harmful led parts of northern Nigeria to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0040073">stop vaccinating for almost a year</a>. This led to a small outbreak that spread from that area to other countries.</p>

<p>Research shows that false news online travels “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aap9559">farther, faster, deeper and more broadly</a> than the truth.”</p>

<p>Unfortunately, misinformation could also contribute to a resurgence of polio in places where it has been eliminated – even the U.S. <a href="https://theconversation.com/even-small-drops-in-vaccination-rates-for-us-children-can-lead-to-disease-outbreaks-265555">In Colorado</a>, about 1 in 8 kindergartners <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html">haven’t had all their polio shots</a>. And in 2022, vaccine-derived polio <a href="https://theconversation.com/fears-of-a-polio-resurgence-in-the-us-have-health-officials-on-high-alert-a-virologist-explains-the-history-of-this-dreaded-disease-189107">paralyzed an unvaccinated young man</a> in New York.</p>

<p>Though rumors can travel quickly, trust is built <a href="https://theconversation.com/address-science-misinformation-not-by-repeating-the-facts-but-by-building-conversation-and-community-249121">one conversation at a time</a>, by neighbors, religious leaders and doctors who take parents’ questions and concerns seriously.</p>

<h2>So close to the finish line</h2>

<p>Unfortunately, the budget of the worldwide program to end polio <a href="https://healthpolicy-watch.news/billions-needed-to-rebuild-gazas-health-system-polio-eradication-faces-30-percent-budget-cut/">decreased by 30%</a> in 2026, mostly because wealthy countries cut their foreign aid. This cut is largely led by the U.S., which withdrew from the World Health Organization, or WHO, officially in <a href="https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/united-states-completes-who-withdrawal.html">January 2026</a>. Other wealthy donor governments like <a href="https://www.usnews.com/news/world/articles/2025-12-08/global-leaders-commit-1-9-billion-to-eradicate-polio-amid-funding-cuts">Germany and the U.K.</a> have also made cuts.</p>

<p>The WHO has warned that these cuts mean that in some places, the fight against polio <a href="https://www.al-monitor.com/originals/2025/10/ending-polio-still-possible-health-officials-say-funding-cut-30">will not be able to continue</a>.</p>

<p>Only one human disease has ever been wiped off the planet for good: <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/smallpox/about/history.html">smallpox</a>, in 1980. Polio <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/global-polio-vaccination/about/index.html">could be the second</a>. The world has never been this close.</p>

<p>Somewhere today, a healthcare worker is coloring another tiny pinkie purple. Each one breaks a link in the chain that polio needs to survive.</p>

<title>Nathaniel Hawthorne’s notebooks reveal the strange workings of his imagination</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767336/original/file-20261020-70-cfdq1j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=180%2C61%2C4914%2C3276&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">After Hawthorne&#39;s death, his wife, Sophia, described the short ideas and fantasies that he jotted down as &#39;so very near the creative soul of the artist.&#39;</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/painting-of-nathaniel-hawthorne-hangs-in-the-parlor-room-at-news-photo/983722020?phrase=nathaniel%20hawthorne&amp;adppopup=true">Barry Chin/The Boston Globe via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://library.northshore.edu/c.php?g=895745&amp;p=6442249">After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825</a>, 21-year-old Nathaniel Hawthorne returned to his family home in Salem, Massachusetts, to live with his mother and two sisters. </p>

<p>Over the next two decades, the aspiring author took on just two short-term jobs. Otherwise, he spent much of his time as a recluse: reading, taking long walks in Salem, socializing with a small group of friends, and writing stories and sketches from the third-story bedroom of the home he called “<a href="https://7gables.org/salem-beyond/meet-hawthorne-and-friends/">Castle Dismal</a>.” During that period and beyond, Hawthorne kept a series of notebooks, which scholars see as an important primary source for understanding the ideas and descriptions that informed his early writings and later novels.</p>

<p>Mainly, however, the notebooks served as a writer’s repository: Hawthorne could let his imagination wander freely without having to worry about being called unconventional, depressive or mad.</p>

<p>For over three decades <a href="https://english.umd.edu/directory/robert-levine">as a Hawthorne scholar</a>, I’ve used the notebooks – later titled “<a href="https://books.google.com/books/about/The_Centenary_Edition_of_the_Works_of_Na.html?id=ca_O0QEACAAJ">The American Notebooks</a>” – to help me prepare editions and scholarly monographs. But I’ve long been intrigued by the notebooks’ shortest entries. Often no more than a single paragraph, they make up fewer than 10,000 of the 200,000 words found in “The American Notebooks.” They are weird and captivating, and in their own way seem like what we now call <a href="https://www.writingclasses.com/toolbox/ask-writer/what-is-flash-fiction">flash fiction</a> or <a href="https://www.nycmidnight.com/howtowritemicrofiction">microfiction</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-right ">
            <img alt="Book cover reading 'Nathaniel Hawthorne: Parables, Fantasies, Fragments' with an image of a Hawthorne's visage chopped up into squares and rearranged." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767337/original/file-20261020-50-l5zbne.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767337/original/file-20261020-50-l5zbne.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=905&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767337/original/file-20261020-50-l5zbne.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=905&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767337/original/file-20261020-50-l5zbne.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=905&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767337/original/file-20261020-50-l5zbne.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1138&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767337/original/file-20261020-50-l5zbne.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1138&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767337/original/file-20261020-50-l5zbne.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1138&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://cdn2.penguin.com.au/covers/original/9781598538618.jpg">Library of America</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Hawthorne published collections of his tales and sketches <a href="https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/13707">in 1837</a> <a href="https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/512">and 1846</a>, which included such macabre and bleak tales: “<a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/Young-Goodman-Brown">Young Goodman Brown</a>,” “<a href="https://americanliterature.com/author/nathaniel-hawthorne/short-story/the-ministers-black-veil">The Minister’s Black Veil</a>” and “<a href="https://www.columbia.edu/itc/english/f1124y-001/resources/The_Birthmark.pdf">The Birth-mark</a>.” In 1850, at the age of 46, he published his first novel, “<a href="https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/25344">The Scarlet Letter</a>,” which established him as one of the leading American writers of his day.</p>

<p>After Hawthorne’s death in 1864, his wife, <a href="https://library.northshore.edu/c.php?g=895894&amp;p=6555322">Sophia</a>, began transcribing “The American Notebooks” for The Atlantic Monthly. In the process, she grew fond of the fragments, likening them to sketches that bring us “so very near the creative soul of the artist.” </p>

<p>I have collected 200 of the most compelling of these fragments <a href="https://www.loa.org/books/parables-fantasies-fragments">for an edition</a> that was published by the Library of America in October 2026.</p>

<p>Consider the following fragment, which has no relation to anything that Hawthorne actually published: </p>

<blockquote>
<p>“To have one event operate in several places – as, for example, if a man’s head were to be cut off in the town, men’s heads to drop off in several other towns.”</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Phrased as if for a story that would never be written, this jotting, complete in itself, conjures an eerie world in which violence toward one person reverberates through other people in other places, leaving human bodies mysteriously linked. </p>

<p>In a fragment written in 1836, Hawthorne fantasizes about upending social conventions:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>“Would it not be wiser for people to rejoice in all they now sorrow for? – and vice versa. To put on bridal garments at funerals, and mourning at weddings. For their friends to condole with them, when they attained riches or power, as only so much care added &amp;c.”</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Hawthorne never wrote a story about women wearing bridal garments at funerals. But the stand-alone fragment, in the seeming spirit of <a href="https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/june-3-1924-franz-kafka-dies/">Franz Kafka’s surreal and unsettling fiction</a>, links success to misery, and happiness to death.   </p>

<p>That Hawthorne could be regarded as a precursor to Kafka, <a href="https://thebaffler.com/latest/kafka-in-pieces-goldman">who wrote posthumously published fragments</a>, was first articulated by the Argentinian modernist <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1986/06/15/obituaries/jorge-luis-borges-a-master-of-fantasy-and-fable-is-dead.html">Jorge Luis Borges</a> in his 1949 lecture “<a href="https://utpress.utexas.edu/9780292760028/">Nathaniel Hawthorne</a>.” For Borges, Hawthorne prefigured Kafka in his commitment to “pure fantasies that do not look for a justification or moral and that seem to have no other substance than an obscure terror.”</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Black and white photo of old, clapboard colonial homes packed tightly together on a side street." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767329/original/file-20261020-50-kuq4am.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767329/original/file-20261020-50-kuq4am.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767329/original/file-20261020-50-kuq4am.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767329/original/file-20261020-50-kuq4am.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767329/original/file-20261020-50-kuq4am.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767329/original/file-20261020-50-kuq4am.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767329/original/file-20261020-50-kuq4am.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://lostnewengland.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/2462_1890-1910c-pem.jpg">Frank Cousins Glass Plate Negatives Collection</a></span>

<p>Borges’ assessment seems especially apt for the parables, fantasies and fragments that can be found in Hawthorne’s “American Notebooks,” many of which evoke a hidden menace or unsettling plot:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>“A stove possessed by a Devil.”  </p>

<p>“Follow out the fantasy of a person’s taking his life by installments, 
instead of at one payment – say ten years of life alternately with ten years of
suspended animation.”</p>

<p>“Little gnomes dwelling in hollow teeth; they find a tooth that has been      plugged with gold, and it serves them as a gold mine.”</p>
</blockquote>

<p>In a longer fragment, written in 1853, Hawthorne anticipates the many horror films featuring a demonic or possessed child:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>“A family, consisting of a father, mother, and two children, are out for a walk, 
and sitting together in a wood. The little girl rambles away into the wood – they
call for her – within a brief time, she comes back. At first, they notice no difference in her; but by degrees, they begin to see something odd – they notice more and more, till, in the course of years, they almost suspect that it was not their own child, but a strange child, who came back.”</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Hawthorne, who had two daughters and a son, captures how children can seem to their parents like mysterious little people beyond their control. He would explore this dynamic in Pearl, the willful child in “The Scarlet Letter.” At one point, Pearl’s mother, Hester Prynne, wonders whether she’s a “demon offspring.”</p>

<p>Hawthorne’s notebook fragments are wide-ranging, but certain themes repeatedly crop up: the psychology of divided selves, tensions between men and women and even possibilities for a better world. As he hopefully imagines in a stand-alone fragment: “Cannon transformed to church-bells.” </p>

<p>Who was Hawthorne the writer? A neo-Puritan moralist? A social realist? A modernist? A romancer? The fragments complicate rather than answer such questions. In his preface to “<a href="https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25344/25344-h/25344-h.htm">The Scarlet Letter</a>,” Hawthorne remarks on his desire to “keep the inmost Me behind its veil.” </p>

<p>But with the help of the fragments, we get behind the veil, at least a bit – and glimpse something like what Sophia believed was the spirit informing Hawthorne’s writing.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294421/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

excerpt: After Hawthorne's death, his wife, Sophia, described the short ideas and fantasies that he jotted down as 'so very near the creative soul of the artist.' Barry
body: After Hawthorne's death, his wife, Sophia, described the short ideas and fantasies that he jotted down as 'so very near the creative soul of the artist.' Barry Chin/The Boston Globe via Getty Images After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825 , 21-year-old Nathaniel Hawthorne returned to his family home in Salem, Massachusetts, to live with his mother and two sisters
Over the next two decades, the aspiring author took on just two short-term jobs

Otherwise, he spent much of his time as a recluse: reading, taking long walks in Salem, socializing with a small group of friends, and writing stories and sketches from the third-story bedroom of the home he called “ Castle Dismal .” During that period and beyond, Hawthorne kept a series of notebooks, which scholars see as an important primary source for understanding the ideas and descriptions that informed his early writings and later novels
Mainly, however, the notebooks served as a writer’s repository: Hawthorne could let his imagination wander freely without having to worry about being called unconventional, depressive or mad
For over three decades as a Hawthorne scholar , I’ve used the notebooks – later titled “ The American Notebooks ” – to help me prepare editions and scholarly monographs
But I’ve long been intrigued by the notebooks’ shortest entries

Often no more than a single paragraph, they make up fewer than 10,000 of the 200,000 words found in “The American Notebooks.” They are weird and captivating, and in their own way seem like what we now call flash fiction or microfiction . ‘Nathaniel Hawthorne: Parables, Fantasies, Fragments’ features 200 short selections from the author’s notebooks

Library of America Hawthorne published collections of his tales and sketches in 1837 and 1846 , which included such macabre and bleak tales: “ Young Goodman Brown ,” “ The Minister’s Black Veil ” and “ The Birth-mark .” In 1850, at the age of 46, he published his first novel, “ The Scarlet Letter ,” which established him as one of the leading American writers of his day
After Hawthorne’s death in 1864, his wife, Sophia , began transcribing “The American Notebooks” for The Atlantic Monthly

In the process, she grew fond of the fragments, likening them to sketches that bring us “so very near the creative soul of the artist.” I have collected 200 of the most compelling of these fragments for an edition that was published by the Library of America in October 2026

Consider the following fragment, which has no relation to anything that Hawthorne actually published: “To have one event operate in several places – as, for example, if a man’s head were to be cut off in the town, men’s heads to drop off in several other towns.” Phrased as if for a story that would never be written, this jotting, complete in itself, conjures an eerie world in which violence toward one person reverberates through other people in other places, leaving human bodies mysteriously linked
In a fragment written in 1836, Hawthorne fantasizes about upending social conventions: “Would it not be wiser for people to rejoice in all they now sorrow for? – and vice versa
To put on bridal garments at funerals, and mourning at weddings
For their friends to condole with them, when they attained riches or power, as only so much care added &c.” Hawthorne never wrote a story about women wearing bridal garments at funerals
But the stand-alone fragment, in the seeming spirit of Franz Kafka’s surreal and unsettling fiction , links success to misery, and happiness to death

That Hawthorne could be regarded as a precursor to Kafka, who wrote posthumously published fragments , was first articulated by the Argentinian modernist Jorge Luis Borges in his 1949 lecture “ Nathaniel Hawthorne .” For Borges, Hawthorne prefigured Kafka in his commitment to “pure fantasies that do not look for a justification or moral and that seem to have no other substance than an obscure terror.” Nathaniel Hawthorne spent much of his childhood and young adult years living with his mother and sisters in a three-story home on Herbert Street in Salem that he dubbed ‘Castle Dismal.’ Frank Cousins Glass Plate Negatives Collection Borges’ assessment seems especially apt for the parables, fantasies and fragments that can be found in Hawthorne’s “American Notebooks,” many of which evoke a hidden menace or unsettling plot: “A stove possessed by a Devil.” “Follow out the fantasy of a person’s taking his life by installments, instead of at one payment – say ten years of life alternately with ten years of suspended animation.” “Little gnomes dwelling in hollow teeth; they find a tooth that has been plugged with gold, and it serves them as a gold mine.” In a longer fragment, written in 1853, Hawthorne anticipates the many horror films featuring a demonic or possessed child: “A family, consisting of a father, mother, and two children, are out for a walk, and sitting together in a wood
The little girl rambles away into the wood – they call for her – within a brief time, she comes back

At first, they notice no difference in her; but by degrees, they begin to see something odd – they notice more and more, till, in the course of years, they almost suspect that it was not their own child, but a strange child, who came back.” Hawthorne, who had two daughters and a son, captures how children can seem to their parents like mysterious little people beyond their control

He would explore this dynamic in Pearl, the willful child in “The Scarlet Letter.” At one point, Pearl’s mother, Hester Prynne, wonders whether she’s a “demon offspring.” Hawthorne’s notebook fragments are wide-ranging, but certain themes repeatedly crop up: the psychology of divided selves, tensions between men and women and even possibilities for a better world

As he hopefully imagines in a stand-alone fragment: “Cannon transformed to church-bells.” Who was Hawthorne the writer? A neo-Puritan moralist? A social realist? A modernist? A romancer? The fragments complicate rather than answer such questions

In his preface to “ The Scarlet Letter ,” Hawthorne remarks on his desire to “keep the inmost Me behind its veil.” But with the help of the fragments, we get behind the veil, at least a bit – and glimpse something like what Sophia believed was the spirit informing Hawthorne’s writing
