title: Trump’s vicious closing message in Michigan
excerpt: The day after former President Barack Obama and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigned together in Detroit, President Donald Trump launched an anti
body: The day after former President Barack Obama and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigned together in Detroit, President Donald Trump launched an anti-Muslim attack against El-Sayed. | Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s midterm barnstorming is getting uglier and more desperate.  What’s happening? At a campaign rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, Trump launched a new round of anti-Muslim attacks against Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, describing him as a “jihadist” who “should never be allowed inside the halls of our great beautiful Capitol.”  “If Abdul and the Democrats win,” Trump told supporters , “they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.” What’s the context? Trump’s speech marks the crescendo — so far — of what has become an increasingly Islamophobic midterm campaign by the Republican Party, centered on El-Sayed

Mike Rogers, Michigan’s Republican Senate nominee, has repeatedly tried to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, and Republicans have also attempted to wield Islamophobia against the Democratic Party as a whole
Greg Abbott told Fox News that his Democratic opponent, Gina Hinojosa, “supports Sharia law,” while at the Republican midterm convention in September, Texas Sen
Ted Cruz said that “communism” and “Islamism” were allying against Republicans

What’s the big picture? In addition to his overt Islamophobia, Trump’s presence on the campaign trail in the final few weeks of the midterm elections has been decidedly strange and surprisingly heavy on physical descriptions of Sen

Jon Husted (R-OH) .  Now, with just eight days to go, Trump’s itinerary features rallies in Mississippi, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina, and Florida — all Republican states where the party has found itself, to one degree or another, with a tougher-than-expected Senate race on its hands.  It’s hardly the travel schedule of a president who feels good about his party’s chances— such as in Michigan, where El-Sayed is leading in most recent polls
And with that, it’s time to log off… US elections may not be until next week, but two other countries held theirs over the weekend: Serbia and Brazil

As my colleague Caitlin Dewey reports in Vox’s Today, Explained newsletter , both resulted in surprise victories over right-wing nationalist parties, with Serbia ousting its incumbent strongman, Aleksandar Vučić

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory over Flávio Bolsonaro is also especially good news for the climate: As the New York Times reported earlier this month, the fate of the Amazon rainforest may well have hinged on the outcome of the election
Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: The far-right just lost. Twice.
excerpt: Supporters of Serbia’s Students’ List movement celebrate in Belgrade on October 26, 2026. | Milos Milanovic/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Tod
body: Supporters of Serbia’s Students’ List movement celebrate in Belgrade on October 26, 2026. | Milos Milanovic/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Vox isn’t typically in the business of covering elections in far-flung locales like the central Balkans. (No offense whatsoever to anyone from the central Balkans!) But on Sunday, an insurgent student-backed movement in Serbia successfully toppled the country’s ruling right-wing political machine, creating an unexpected opening for democratic reform.  Then, in another upset halfway around the globe, Brazilian voters reelected incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva over his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro. “Democracy always, dictatorship never again,” Lula said in his victory speech
That’s two big repudiations of the nationalist right in 24 hours

Not quite enough to declare a trend, maybe, but sufficient to remind us that there’s still hope for the world’s embattled democratic institutions.  More than that, these results offer evidence of something that sounds naive and Pollyannish in our current moment, but can (apparently!) still prove true: Organizing can be a powerful force for electoral change — both abroad and maybe here at home
Go a little deeper View Link To be fair, the two elections differed considerably, and I don’t want to suggest it’s all sunshine and democratic renewal ahead for Brazil and Serbia
Bolsonaro is refusing to concede, for instance

And in Serbia, the victorious Student List still has to stand up a government, a prime minister, and a full policy platform — something the nascent movement has never done before.  But academics and elections-watchers in both countries have credited the results in large part to mass protests and grassroots organizing that helped mobilize unexpected numbers of voters
Serbian students began their movement in 2024, following the partial collapse of a railway station that killed 16 people
The government’s failure to fully explain the cause of the collapse — or hold anyone responsible — fueled months of marches, protest bike rides, and other demonstrations
That movement eventually grew into the Student List: an opposition electoral slate that fielded 250 candidates in Sunday’s parliamentary elections.  The story in Brazil is quite different
Lula, the country’s leftist president, was actually poised to lose
Brazil uses a two-round popular vote to elect its president, and if no candidate secures more than half the vote in the first round, then the top two candidates proceed to a runoff election

Lula placed second in that first vote, after Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and the heir to his father’s far-right political movement.  To many Brazilians, that second-place finish served as a kind of wake-up call. “No runoff campaign in Brazil has ever brought so many people to the streets and onto social media,”  Guilherme Casarões , an associate professor of Brazilian studies at Florida International University, wrote in an analysis of the surprise results

One WhatsApp channel dedicated to turning voters out for Lula grew to nearly 11 million followers , up from just 50,000 after his first-round loss.  Looking at these projects abroad, I’m struck that American pro-democracy movements like No Kings haven’t achieved that kind of influence

Arguably, that’s in part a consequence of their failure to turn protest energy into actual political organizing — things like registering voters, knocking on doors, and fielding candidates.  But there are some signs that may be shifting
No Kings has lately pivoted its focus, for instance, from mostly organizing protests to urging Americans — of both parties — to vote in the midterms
And Indivisible, one of the groups behind the movement, claims that early voting surged during the latest protests in the zip codes where they occurred
It’s not exactly a central Balkan moment, but maybe it’s a hint of things to come

Just ask a Serb or a Brazilian.  One link for later ➨ Leave your big life decisions to chance. (Sort of.) A team of researchers invited people to make a big life decision by flipping a coin and then tracked their happiness with the outcome
They found that, of the people who obeyed the results of the toss, the ones who changed something big were overwhelmingly happier

That doesn’t literally mean we should all resort to coin tosses, but it should tell us something important: We often tend to be too cautious about making major changes .  Before you go… Did you know… that in the 1870s and ’80s, spectators flocked to Madison Square Garden for long-distance walking competitions ? Athletes walked up to 600 miles in six days, just going round and round the stadium.  Today’s trivia: Which New Jersey city was the first predominantly white community in the US to vote in favor of school integration? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the radioactive noble gas with the chemical symbol Rn
That would be radon, once a trendy (deadly) ingredient in quack medicines .

title: Why Democrats are pivoting to thirst traps
excerpt: “It is a very real dynamic that you could have all these videos about Jon Ossoff, and it's not seen as detracting away from his overall message or his seriousne
body: “It is a very real dynamic that you could have all these videos about Jon Ossoff, and it's not seen as detracting away from his overall message or his seriousness as a politician,” The 19th’s Grace Panetta said on Vox’s Today, Explained podcast. | Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images Democrats have been emphasizing lots of issues in the runup to the 2026 midterms: The Iran war

Specifically, their candidates: The internet is awash in clips of Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed pumping iron and podcasters proclaiming that “America deserves a hot president” in a video interspersed with photos of Georgia Sen
Having a good-looking candidate is by no means a new tactic — famously, it may have helped John F

Kennedy win election over Richard Nixon — but the online left is adapting that strategy for the internet and fandom age.  Grace Panetta, a politics reporter for The 19th, wrote about how “thirst edits” of Ossoff in particular are proliferating online

Panetta says the organic origins of a lot of these videos are of particular interest to Democratic operatives, who see it as a way to gain back ground they lost on the internet after the 2024 election

Panetta spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about who’s thirsting over Democratic politicians in the first place, how 2026’s hot candidates are different from those of yore, and whether it’s actually giving them a boost.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Where are these edits coming from? Regular online creators
And it’s important to note at the outset that these are not paid partnerships
The campaign is not paying these influencers to make edits about how they think their candidate’s really attractive.  That’s partly why I wanted to dig into it, because it’s organic
These are just online creators wanting to draw visibility and attention to a candidate that they really like
Jon Ossoff is currently running for reelection in these midterms

How do we know for sure that he isn’t somehow behind the campaign? I spoke to several creators who make these videos and they said that they’re doing it for the love of the game and they’re just supporters
His campaign did not give me a quote or a statement for this story
So it’s fair to assume that he’s not directly involved and he doesn’t repost these videos.  But as people pointed out to me, his campaign knows that they have an attractive, compelling candidate
And they’ve previously been vaunted for their digital strategy this cycle of putting out very high-quality livestreams of his rallies
There’s a lot of material for an enterprising TikToker who wants to make these edits or clips
His campaign, as one person put it, is definitely playing into that, but not directly engaging
Is it just an Ossoff thing or is this going on with other candidates? I do recall that Abdul El-Sayed hits the gym
I just watched so many videos for this story
I also came across a fair number of Gavin Newsom edits
There are people who think he gives sort of a Patrick Bateman, American Psycho vibe

There are also official Democratic accounts, including the TikTok account for the DNC, the headquarters account, which was formerly Kamala HQ, who have been posting edits of Ossoff and also Abdul El-Sayed, who kind of leans into this gym-bro persona.  The headquarters account posted a side-by-side of Ossoff and Abdul El-Sayed with the caption, “There are 69 days until election day.” Nice
There are also lots of edits of Mamdani, and former President Barack Obama
Obama nostalgia content goes hard on the internet
So you’re seeing these more official side Democratic campaign accounts leaning into it and playing up their candidates
Having an attractive candidate is nothing new

What feels different about what you’re seeing now on social media? I think this is really a culmination of a lot of different things happening right now in politics and specifically within the Democratic Party.  After their loss in 2024, there was a lot of conversation about the gerontocracy, how we’re governed by a lot of really old people, for the most part, in this century

And also about Democrats’ digital strategy and the aftermath of 2024.  One thing that a lot of people in that digital space have been talking about is how Republicans and the Trump campaign really capitalized on getting that organic engagement on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, where a lot of Americans are now going to get at least some of their news, and also engaging with and encouraging the creation of this kind of organic content on platforms and from creators that are not always expressly political or official-side.  “A candidate’s messaging strategy is only as good as the content and only if it meets people where they are and actually speaks to a real need people have.” As one Democrat I talked to put it, she thinks it’s a way for Democrats to win back the internet and to really create a contrast with the Republicans
And she said to have fun on the internet because Republicans are having fun on the internet and it appears to be working for them, or at least it was in 2024
Is there something about this being something on the left that makes it sort of tricky? This is, broadly speaking, objectification, right? It is a fine line between thirst and objectification

And there is also a gendered element to it that it is mostly men that these types of videos are being made about.  Now, granted, a lot of people make sort of hype edits or positive content about AOC because she’s a very popular female politician on the left, but it’s true that women candidates are held to higher standards in terms of how they present themselves and how their supporters portray them.  It is a very real dynamic that you could have all these videos about Jon Ossoff, and it’s not seen as detracting away from his overall message or his seriousness as a politician

Is there a drawback of focusing on looks? Does it make the Democratic Party or these candidates seem superficial or not that serious? President Trump has been the defining figure in our politics for 10 years now
And he is famously very, very image focused and image obsessed
We live in a very image-obsessed society, and I think there’s kind of a bipartisan acknowledgement of that
And looks matter to people in all kinds of ways
They do matter in politics, they do matter to voters
Whether you like that that’s the case or not, it is the reality
And I think the way that a lot of people on the left see this is, people want to look at attractive people
People take attractive people more seriously and are more willing to listen to them

title: The Democrat capturing Christian voters in the Trump era
excerpt: ELLSWORTH, Kansas — David Rankin has never been one for putting up campaign lawn signs
body: ELLSWORTH, Kansas — David Rankin has never been one for putting up campaign lawn signs
As a lifelong Republican in a town of 3,000 — where Donald Trump has won by 50-point margins since 2016 — he’s never seen a reason to put a candidate’s name in his yard
But recently, Rankin and his wife Dina did something new
Frustrated with their senators in Washington, DC, they went out to their front lawn and hammered in a sign in support of the Rev
Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor running for US Senate — and a Democrat
As signs of a midterm blue wave rise around the country, perhaps no state has been more surprising to watch than Kansas, a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years
A string of polls now show the incumbent GOP Sen

Roger Marshall locked in a tight race for survival, buffeted by low approval ratings, a string of personal controversies, poor campaigning, and Trump’s unpopularity over healthcare cuts, fuel costs, beef prices , and tariffs.  Kansas is now a toss-up, attracting both national attention and last-minute cash investments from the national parties
Pundits have pointed to a range of reasons: the national backlash against the president; the unusual weakness of Marshall’s candidacy; the persistence of pocketbook issues for Kansas voters
But there’s also something more interesting afoot, a difference that may have its own national repercussions

Hamilton’s campaign is a rare instance of a Democrat deliberately rallying people of faith, boldly proclaiming the Gospels, openly talking about Jesus Christ, and asking voters to find — and embrace — a profoundly Democratic message in the beliefs they profess every Sunday. “Our faith is respectful…it reflects the ideas of justice and fairness, things that are just fundamental to the Bible,” Hamilton told me in early October. “Two thousand verses in the Bible talk about poverty and taking care of the poor
That’s not what you hear from Christian nationalists.” That was part of the draw for the Rankins
They had known about Hamilton for a while
Friends had been to his church, and David — a retired choir director — told me that his own Presbyterian congregation had used Hamilton’s books and various sermon series as part of their Bible study

So when they found out Hamilton had decided to run earlier this year — as a Democrat, no less — they prepared themselves for the possibility that they might have to break with their political party this year. “Things are not right right now

They’re not right in Washington and we have to do better,”  Rankin told me. “His faith is just going to make him better as he serves us.” If Hamilton, and a handful of other candidates of faith in nearby Iowa and Texas, win, it could signal a shift in US politics — or at least a tremor in one of its most rock-solid certainties

One of the defining stories of the last century has been the realignment of religion, religious life, and religious voters on the political spectrum — and the complete shift of evangelicals toward the GOP

From the 1960s to the 1980s , Democrats could routinely count on majority support among white evangelical Protestants in congressional elections, and at least substantial support from them at the presidential level

But by the 1990s — with Americans becoming more evangelical and evangelicals becoming more Republican — the GOP had effectively locked in a permanent voting bloc, especially powerful in the heartland and the South

Meanwhile the opposite has been true for the Democratic Party: Rapid liberalization and secularization has moved nonreligious and anti-religious voters toward the Democrats, while religious Democratic voters tend to come from smaller progressive churches
The shift has only accelerated in recent years, as Trump has consolidated evangelical voters, while white college-educated voters — who are largely secular — moved left

And when blue-state Democrats try to deploy faith-based messages, they get derided or dismissed as awkward, disingenuous, or off-brand.  The result: In recent years, Democrats have mostly ceded religious voters, outreach, and messaging to Republicans
That has made it almost impossible for the party to compete in red and rural states, where white evangelical voters make up a substantial share of the electorate
In turn, Democrats have faced increasingly long odds to win those Senate seats, or expand the electoral map in presidential contests

Whether he wins or loses in Kansas, Hamilton’s overperforming campaign poses a high-stakes question for Democrats nationally: Can a true moderate, a self-described radical centrist, and an openly religious person offer a road map for reclaiming Christianity and winning back religious voters?  Maybe Hamilton does represent such a playbook
But to watch him on the trail, you find another fact that makes his path look much harder for other Democrats to walk
It’s not just that Hamilton is a religious Democrat, or even that he’s mastered a message for religious swing voters hoping to reconcile their faith with a Democratic candidate
He’s also a deeply talented public speaker, well-connected community leader, and authoritative religious voice willing — unlike most pastors — to wade directly into electoral politics

He’s the leader of a very unique church — not just a politician “affiliated” with Christianity or training to join the clergy, but an established figure in an established institutional denomination that insulates him against attacks on his faith and character. (One of those came from no less than Vice President JD Vance, who attacked Hamilton in September as “dressed in the skin suit of our religion.”) The skills that come with leading a megachurch also lend themselves easily to campaigning — but might not be replicable for others, at least not to this extent
And Hamilton has managed to ease concerns from secular or nonreligious liberals, without compromising his centrist, at times heterodox, religious and political beliefs
His campaign could change control of Congress
But beyond that, it also offers a new, possibly more effective, political language for Democrats in a post-Trump world

On a recent Thursday in Hutchinson, Kansas, Adam Hamilton found himself therapizing a crowd of several hundred. “Republicans for Hamilton” pins floated in the audience at this downtown theater in the middle of the state, as he diagnosed the problems in Washington that have bled into Kansas
Members of the US Senate, Hamilton said gently, had become like Dorothy’s traveling companions in The Wizard of Oz : They’d lost their minds, their hearts, and their courage
Along the way, he said, they, and President Donald Trump, had torn apart the fabric of the community, turning neighbors into suspicious strangers
Heads nodded in agreement; those closest to me sighed and lowered their heads
Hamilton recounted something a mother once asked him: to be “somebody who’s going to help me not hate my neighbors with the red caps anymore.” “And she wasn’t talking about Chiefs fans,” he quipped
To see Hamilton in action feels like being thrown back to a forgotten era of politics: His tone is conciliatory
He’s eager to dispense with the “extremes.” He slips into preaching about “radical love,” and he’s comfortable quoting scripture and referencing Christian teachings when answering policy questions
Time permitting, he shakes hands and greets everyone in a room

title: Gen Z has buyer’s remorse on Trump
excerpt: Florida A&M University students of Alpha Phi Alpha, Inc. walk to the election polls on October 15, 2026, in Tallahassee, Florida. | Jeffery D
body: Florida A&M University students of Alpha Phi Alpha, Inc. walk to the election polls on October 15, 2026, in Tallahassee, Florida. | Jeffery D
Adams/Florida A&M University via Getty Images If there is a Democratic wave in next week’s midterm elections, one of the biggest reasons for that will be young voters

While voters of all ages have soured on President Donald Trump and the Republican Party since his 2024 victory, polls show that the decline has been particularly pronounced among the young people who’d backed him in surprising numbers just two years ago

That election result prompted endless conversation about a “vibe shift” among Gen Z, and whether younger voters had turned against “woke” progressives , become radicalized by “manosphere” podcasts and TikTok algorithms , or lashed out against Biden-era gerontocracy
But the story looks very different heading into November

A Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month found that, of people aged 19–34 who voted for Trump over Kamala Harris, only 49 percent approve of his job performance as president. (In contrast, among Trump 2024 voters aged 50 and above, about 75 percent still approve of him.) Pew also found earlier this year that partisan identification among young adults has shifted — or, rather, reverted.  In 2022 and 2023, Democrats had a 17-point advantage among adults aged 18–29 — 55 percent of them said they were Democrats or leaned toward Democrats, while just 38 percent said they were Republican or leaned toward the GOP
In 2024, that gap closed, and Republicans actually took a slight edge, 47 percent to Democrats’ 46 percent
But now, in 2026, Democrats are back to a 16-point advantage, getting 54 percent of young voters compared to the GOP’s 38 percent
And it isn’t just that fewer young people are saying they’re Republican
Those who remain Republican are also saying they’re less likely to vote this year
According to the Harvard Youth Poll released last week, 50 percent of Democrats aged 18–29 say they’ll definitely vote, but only 34 percent of Republicans in that age range say the same
That’s a 16-point partisan gap; the biggest this poll found in recent midterm cycles
The core reasons for all this in a sense aren’t too surprising
Like older voters, young voters say they’re most concerned about issues like the cost of living, corruption in government, overseas wars, and the cost of health care

But the swings — and the feelings of betrayal and disappointment among prior Trump supporters — have been particularly dramatic among the young, which raises the question of what about their experience and outlook is influencing their politics in particular.  To answer that, I spoke to advocates and political consultants focused on young voters
Here’s what they see as the origins — and limits — of the coming youthquake

How to think about the Gen Z “Trump regretters” Rachel Janfaza , founder of the Gen Z-focused strategy firm The Up and Up, told me that we should think about young people who voted for Trump in 2024 as really three separate cohorts
First, she said, are the “hardcore MAGA young people who still stand by the president, just like the older MAGA folks.” They supported him in 2024, and they still do

Second, she said, are the young people who “are very much on the America First train” but who “resent the fact that Trump’s basically become part of the establishment, whether it comes to building a White House ballroom, or the Epstein files, or starting new wars” — and have moved away from him as a result
These young people are much less likely to move toward Democrats, but many of them could be disillusioned and not bother to vote this year

Third, she said, is “a large cohort of young people, predominantly young men, who were never hardcore MAGA, but who voted for Trump in 2024 because they were frustrated by the political conversation at large.”  “They were frustrated by their economic situation; they were tired of political correctness and the pendulum swinging too far in the direction of ‘wokeness,’” Janfaza continued

These people, she said, now feel “politically homeless.” Tina Tang of the Democratic-aligned firm Navigator Research has conducted many focus groups interviewing young people who now regret voting for Trump

She told me that many of those “Trump regretters” said they’d initially hoped he would bring change to the political system generally, and that he’d deliver on his promises about the economy and jobs.  “Young voters are especially worried about jobs right now,” Tang said. “That was actually one of the biggest frustrations we heard from young voters this time around: frustration with the job market
We hear a lot about how he promised a lot of things; he promised the economy was going to get better, that costs were going to come down, that there would be more jobs.” Young people are pragmatists
They’re losing faith in the system because they think it isn’t delivering

Several of those I interviewed also urged caution about the common trope that young people tend to be strongly progressive or liberal, a longtime assumption that led many observers to be caught off guard by their swing toward Republicans in 2024

Indeed, the Harvard Youth poll released this week found that 25 percent of 18- to 29-year-olds thought of themselves as liberal, 23 percent as conservative, and about 46 percent as something in between

Santiago Mayer, founder of the progressive youth-focused group Voters of Tomorrow, told me that while Gen Z voters often have liberal values and policy views, they often didn’t define politics in ideological terms: “I think for a lot of things many of us would consider progressive, for them, they are common sense, and they’re not necessarily analyzing these issues through a political lens.” Indeed, Mayer said that while the politicians who are most appealing to young voters can vary in ideology, “the one thing they have in common is that they are very pragmatic and very practical

They are talking about how they’re going to improve things today and how they’re actually going to create material, tangible change in young people’s lives.” Tang of Navigator Research concurred, telling me that young people are “absolutely still very skeptical of both parties.” She added: “What we hear from young people a lot is: they want to see results.” And the results they crave are, above all, about the economy and cost of living

Janfaza told me that there’s been a longtime misconception among pundits that young voters are obsessed with identity and the culture war — but, she argues, that was never quite true, and it’s even less true now. “Now, climate and abortion do not even make it into the top issues that young people are saying they care about,” Janfaza said. “And it doesn’t mean that they don’t care about those issues, but the economic concern just ranks much higher.” Indeed, she believes that the “ flirtation with socialism ” among some young voters is really more about policies such as affordable housing, affordable health care, and affordable education — as well as a promise to break with the status quo. “That’s really what young people are hungry for.”  Key to young people’s worldview is that they’re feeling increasingly pessimistic about that status quo

One striking finding in the Harvard Youth Poll was that, when asked whether they expected to be financially better or worse off than their parents when they reach their age, more said worse — a first-time finding for the poll. “I think you see that in the numbers that there’s a level of nihilism amongst young voters,” Mayer said. “They’re basically giving Democrats another chance
But I worry that this is kind of our last chance to get them to believe in democracy.”  And, he worried, if Democrats don’t deliver actual improvements to their lives, “they’ll be gone for good.”

title: When AI agents run your life
excerpt: An advertisement for Meta's personal AI agent app Muse at a BART station in San Francisco on October 15, 2026. | Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images There are so
body: An advertisement for Meta's personal AI agent app Muse at a BART station in San Francisco on October 15, 2026. | Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images There are some days when there’s so much that needs to get done, I daydream about having a clone of myself
Between paying bills, life admin like renewing my driver’s license, keeping up with doctor’s appointments, and planning meals, it’s a lot
And that doesn’t even begin to touch the work that goes into making a podcast or managing my social life
This feeling of overwhelm resonates with Sari Azout

She’s a mom of three who works in tech. “There is just so much doing,” she told Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast. “I wake up, and I have to do meal coordination and get my kids up for breakfast, coordinate carpools
Then a lot of work during the day, but there’s the email from the teacher, there’s the 20 group chats asking if you want to participate in this group gift
They don’t call it ‘the invisible load’ for no reason.’” Silicon Valley says it has a fix for this kind of mental overload
They don’t want to clone us — at least not yet

But they do think they have the next best thing: AI agents.  Azuot was skeptical when she first got an invite to try an agent, but she says she eventually came around on the technology after back-to-school shopping snuck up on her
She used her agent to get it done. “It blew me away,” she said.  “I remember that night coming home just feeling so calm and reading my son a book and feeling present

And I was like, ‘Wow, I actually was very cynical about something that is giving me more time for living.’” Azout’s experience is, more or less, the sales pitch for AI agents: They’ll help you save time with everyday tasks, so you have more of it for what you want to do

But what are agents, exactly? Are they really all that? And what do we gain — and give up — when we use the technology?   On this week’s episode of Explain It to Me , I spoke with Reece Rogers, a senior software reporter at Wired, to find out

Rogers says to think of agents as the next evolution of AI chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT.  “I’d create this mental model of a tiny digital assistant that’s constantly searching the web, going through your email, and checking your calendar, trying to find ways it could proactively be helpful for you,” he explains. “Agents are more proactive
It’s scanning your email 24/7 and sending you a message, maybe highlighting a potential calendar conflict.” Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Rogers, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545

What agents are out there right now? At the start of this year, there was a tool called OpenClaw that really sparked this with early adopters in San Francisco, but now there are much more consumer-friendly versions, with one of the most notable being Meta’s Muse.  There’s also a tool from OpenAI called Dots
But where Meta’s Muse is free to download, OpenAI’s Dots is still behind a $100/month paywall.  You tried an AI agent for a recent story you wrote
How was that experience? One personal example, to share something that I’ve actually been using agents for, is our couch
It’s broken, and finding a new couch has been a pain
We want a sleeper bed, but we want these specific colors
I’ve been using Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots to try to find a few different options for us.  One interesting thing is that Meta’s Muse is connected to Facebook Marketplace

There are these really good integrations where I can give it all these details, and it found a few good couches that are only maybe a couple blocks from me.  I really enjoyed OpenAI’s Dots experience as well
I spent about an hour talking to it on the phone, and the AI agent made a packet of all these different options I could find
Just this morning, it flagged that one of them is now 40 percent off.  Is that how this tech is typically used? Most people are using this as part of a workflow
I attach it to my email, I attach it to my calendar, and I’m using it as a personal assistant to organize my life

But people have been quite creative.  One of the breakout uses for Meta’s Muse is people have been connecting their bank account statements and then using it to scan for subscriptions they might want to cancel
So it can be used in many different ways, though I will say I do not connect it to my own bank account for a myriad of reasons
I’m not going to lie, the idea of giving any third party access to my bank information does not thrill me

That’s one of my biggest concerns about these AI agents: how much personal information we’re handing over to these large companies.  When I tested Meta’s Muse, it wanted access to my email, my bank account, even my passport expiration details

The pitch is convenience, but Muse users are automatically opted in to having all of their interactions with Muse used to train Meta’s AI models.  I would definitely recommend, if you’re sharing personal details, go into the settings and turn that off because you might be handing over even more information about yourself than you initially realize
What is the privacy situation with all of this? We all have various apps where we don’t read and still click “I agree,” but this feels like it could be more invasive
Yes, especially because it’s all about automation

If you’re automating things and it has access to all of your data, it could make mistakes and embarrass you in ways you might not even be thinking about.  There was this one really interesting story of someone who had connected an AI agent to their work Slack in addition to their bank account
And their agent just automatically posted how much money was in their checking account for all of their coworkers to see.  Oh no
So there are these kinds of mistakes that these AI tools can still make

If you’re interested in experimenting with them, I would be really thoughtful with how you’re setting up these tools as well as what kind of information you feel comfortable sharing. “You can see in the marketing that these companies are trying to find some way to entice new users.” How are these AI agents being marketed? AI is not popular right now
Just ask any politician who has a data center coming to their state
How are they trying to sell this to the average person? The AI backlash really is at a fever pitch right now
You could almost see that in the way that AI companies are trying to market these tools

title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
excerpt: Holmes's charm is still unsettling on screen: Even knowing the full Theranos story, the documentary captures how effectively Holmes plants seeds of doubt—j
body: Holmes's charm is still unsettling on screen: Even knowing the full Theranos story, the documentary captures how effectively Holmes plants seeds of doubt—journalists who interviewed her in her prime later admitted she had fooled them completely

Peer review isn't a perfect safety net: Science's built-in fact-checking system has real cracks—10,000 papers were retracted in 2023 alone, and preprint servers, press releases, and social media now routinely bypass it

Reporters face the same vulnerability as investors: Even seasoned science journalists rely on trust and expert opinion to vet claims, raising an uncomfortable question: how confident can anyone really be that they wouldn't have fallen for it too " data-chronoton-post-id="1147610" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.  I went in not really knowing what to expect
I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!)

I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood , and the Hulu series The Dropout , starring Amanda Seyfried
Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled
But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects
The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything
In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19
She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood
Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014
Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old
Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work
Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead
MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015
Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016
That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong
In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors
She began serving her sentence in May 2023
It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children
I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film
As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer , there are plenty of super close-ups
I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people
And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out
Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind
Will anyone believe her? I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence
And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator
You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind
At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat

Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie? But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune ’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT ’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015

Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022
If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all? One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data

Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification
Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process
You should be able to trust published scientific papers
Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance
Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis
Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always
There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence
Many papers ultimately end up with corrections

title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
excerpt: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it
body: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it
For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores

But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability
For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it
Start with the workload, not the model There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture
There is only the right solution for the business problem
A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight
An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures
The constraints should determine the architecture
That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments
During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion

Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic
A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application’s latency requirements
Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn’t
The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload
That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern
It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn’t worth the cost
Engineer the system, not the model Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another
Serving architecture influences memory utilization
Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency
Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value
This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance
During inference, the model’s weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length
As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available
Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive
The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize
Then determine if another bottleneck emerged
Don’t think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn’t to collect them all
The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application’s business requirements
For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question
Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value
Build for change, not today’s benchmark Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today’s leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s
The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances
That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy

Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs
A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset
EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series
It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable
Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models
Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes
